blocks.text: Skirting the glade, and stepping carefully over the trails, they proceeded to set their snares at the openings of three of the main alleys; and for a little while the strokes of their hatchets rang out frostily on the still air as they chopped down fragrant armfuls of the young fir branches.

Each of the three snares was set in this fashion: First they stuck the fir branches into the snow to form a thick green fence on both sides of the trail, with a passage only wide enough for one rabbit at a time to pass through. On each side of this passageway they drove securely a slender stake, notched on the inner face. Over the opening they bent down a springy sapling, securing its top, by a strong cord, to a small wooden cross-piece which was caught and held in the notches of the two uprights. From the under side of this cross-piece was suspended the easy-running noose of copper wire, just ample enough for a rabbit’s head, with the ears lying back, to enter readily.

By the time the snares were set it was near sundown, and the young fir-trees were casting long, pointed, purple shadows. With the drawing on of evening the boy felt stirrings of a wild, predatory instinct. His skin tingled with a still excitement which he did not understand, and he went with a fierce yet furtive wariness, peering into the shadows as if for prey. As he and Andy emerged from the woods, and strode silently down the desolate slopes of the pasture lots, he could think of nothing but his return on the morrow to see what prizes had fallen to his snares. His tenderness of heart, his enlightened sympathy with the four-footed kindred, much of his civilisation, in fact, had vanished for the moment, burnt out in the flame of an instinct handed down to him from his primeval ancestors.

That night the moon rose over the young fir woods, blue-white and glittering as on the night before. The air was of the same biting stillness and vitreous transparency. The magic of it stirred up the same merry madness in the veins of the wild rabbits, and set them to aimless gambolling instead of their usual cautious browsing in the thickets of yellow birch. One by one and two by two the white shapes came drifting down the shadowed alleys and moonlight trails of the fir wood toward the bright glade which they seemed to have adopted, for the time, as their playground. The lanes and ways were many that gave entrance to the glade; and presently some half dozen rabbits came bounding, from different directions, across the radiant open. But on the instant they stopped and sat straight up on their haunches, ears erect, struck with consternation.

There at the mouth of one of the alleys a white form jerked high into the air. It hung, silently struggling, whirling round and round, and at the same time swaying up and down with the bending of the sapling-top from which it swung. The startled spectators had no comprehension of the sight, no signal-code to express the kind of peril it portended, and how to flee from it. They sat gazing in terror. Then, at the next entrance, there shot up into the brilliant air another like horror; and at the next, in the same breath, another. The three hung kicking in a hideous silence.

The spell was broken. The spectators, trembling under the imminence of a doom which they could not understand, vanished with long bounds by the opposite side of the glade. All was still again under the blue-white, wizard scrutiny of the moon but those three kicking shapes. And these, too, in a few minutes hung motionless as the fir-trees and the snow. As the glassy cold took hold upon them they slowly stiffened.

questions.prompt: Why do the fences of fir branches matter to how each snare works?
facilitatorNotes: They funnel one rabbit at a time into the noose. Children can trace the parts in order: fence, notched stakes, bent sapling, cross-piece, noose.
evidence: a passage only wide enough for one rabbit at a time to pass through

questions.prompt: What happens to the boy’s tenderness of heart as evening comes, according to the narrator?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator says a hunting instinct has burned it out “for the moment”. Some readers may doubt that instinct explains it; ask what “for the moment” predicts.
evidence: His tenderness of heart
burnt out in the flame of an instinct handed down to him from his primeval ancestors

questions.prompt: How does Roberts show the snares from the rabbits’ side without explaining them?
facilitatorNotes: The rabbits see only white shapes jerking into the air; readers who watched the snares being built understand what they cannot. Discuss how this changes the moonlit play from the story’s opening.
evidence: no comprehension of the sight, no signal-code to express the kind of peril it portended

days.title: The Moonlight Trails — ending: what the boy sees
days.challenge: Trace a character’s feelings as they change within a single scene.
days.focus: The story ends when the boy looks closely at what the snares have done.
days.context: Overnight, three rabbits have died in the snares. In the morning the boy and Andy return to collect them.
days.contentNote: A fox carries off one rabbit; the boy looks closely at the dead rabbits and weeps.

excerpt.locator: The Moonlight Trails; contiguous excerpt, 4 source blocks; opens “About an hour later a big red fox came trotting into the …”; closes “… grin that was half bewilderment, half indulgent comprehension, philosophically followed the penitent.”.

questions.prompt: How does the fox get the third rabbit when he cannot reach the other two?
facilitatorNotes: The third sapling is slender and hangs lower. The fox has also “scored against his human rivals”, which prepares the boy’s indignation.
evidence: The sapling was slender, and drooped its burden closer to the snow

questions.prompt: What does the boy feel when he first sees a rabbit in a snare, and what does he notice that changes his feeling?
facilitatorNotes: Triumph comes first; then the noose marks, the open mouth and the dead eyes of Andy’s rabbit bring tears. Ask which detail matters most to him.
evidence: a novel and fierce sense of triumph
the cruel marks of the noose

questions.prompt: Andy follows with a grin that is half bewilderment. Does the story ask us to agree with the boy or with Andy?
facilitatorNotes: Calling the boy “the penitent” presents him as sorry for a wrong, while Andy treats snaring as ordinary work. Accept arguments that Roberts respects both, noting that the boy has the last words and action.
evidence: philosophically followed the penitent
We won’t snare any more rabbits, Andy

days.title: The Homesickness of Kehonka — excerpt: a resting place on the route
days.challenge: Move between a distant viewpoint and a close view of a flock.
days.focus: A familiar stop becomes a possible home for two birds.
days.context: A migrating flock reaches the Tantramar marshes in spring. Listen for the difference between what a person below can hear and what the narrator lets us see.

excerpt.locator: The Homesickness of Kehonka; contiguous excerpt, 3 source blocks; opens “The April night, softly chill and full of the sense of thaw, …”; closes “… the shore and cast about for a place to build their nest.”.

questions.prompt: How does the passage make the unseen flock seem present before anyone can see it?
facilitatorNotes: The approaching calls suggest distance and steadily growing nearness. Sound carries the scene.
evidence: honk-a-honk, honk-a-honk

questions.prompt: What makes the little lakes suitable for a night’s rest?
facilitatorNotes: Their thickets and bogs offer seclusion, and the birds can feed there.
evidence: shores so choked with thickets and fenced apart with bogs

questions.prompt: How do two young birds respond differently to the leader’s morning signal?
facilitatorNotes: They ignore the departure and begin looking for a nest site. The group’s route need not be every member’s route.
evidence: they swam to the shore and cast about for a place to build their nest

days.title: The Homesickness of Kehonka — excerpt: two brothers and different longings
days.challenge: Compare behaviour before accepting a label such as tame or wild.
days.focus: The farmer recognises a longing he cannot satisfy.
days.context: Two wild goose brothers have been raised on a farm after their eggs were taken from a nest. Their flight feathers have been clipped. The story now compares their temperaments.
days.contentNote: Roberts invents inherited memories for the bird and a human parallel for the farmer, a convention of the literary animal story of his time.

excerpt.locator: The Homesickness of Kehonka; contiguous excerpt, 3 source blocks; opens “Both the young wild geese were fine males. Their heads and long, …”; closes “… too, caught himself straining his gaze beyond the marsh horizons of Tantramar.”.

questions.prompt: How does Kehonka differ from his brother when the flock is content?
facilitatorNotes: He keeps apart and looks and listens toward the north; his brother is satisfied with the farm.
evidence: always a little apart

questions.prompt: Why is it misleading to assume that Kehonka’s longing makes him the shyest bird?
facilitatorNotes: He takes food from the farmer’s hand when the others will not. Longing for freedom and confidence near a person are different traits.
evidence: He would take oats out of the farmer’s hand

questions.prompt: What begins to connect the farmer’s feelings with Kehonka’s?
facilitatorNotes: The bird’s restless gaze gives shape to the farmer’s own less clearly understood wishes.
evidence: straining his gaze beyond the marsh horizons of Tantramar

days.title: The Homesickness of Kehonka — excerpt: the call is answered
days.challenge: Trace a goal through a failed invitation, an effort and a temporary success.
days.focus: The bird’s longing becomes a journey.
days.context: Spring returns. Kehonka has been unable to join the migrating wild geese, but their calls awaken an intense wish to leave. The adult leads the reading of this longer scene; invite the child to reread a chosen short exchange.
days.contentNote: The bird’s clipped wing affects his flight. The claim that desire causes unusual feather growth is part of this historical story, not a biological explanation.

excerpt.locator: The Homesickness of Kehonka; contiguous excerpt, 3 source blocks; opens “When the winter broke, and the seeping drifts shrank together, and the …”; closes “… was thinking of a nest in the wide emptiness of the North.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the first flock turn away after hearing Kehonka?
facilitatorNotes: Its leader sees farm buildings and suspects danger. The refusal is caution, not knowledge of Kehonka’s character.
evidence: suspected treachery

questions.prompt: What makes Kehonka’s flight difficult even though he can get off the ground?
facilitatorNotes: His wings are unequal in spread, so balancing exhausts him.
evidence: His trouble was not the lack of wing surface, but the lack of balance.

questions.prompt: What shows that the next flock accepts Kehonka?
facilitatorNotes: They rest and feed around him, and he joins them without conflict. A young female also responds to him.
evidence: Kehonka found himself easily accepted as a member of the flock

days.title: The Homesickness of Kehonka — ending: the discourager of quests
days.challenge: Track changes of method while a goal remains the same.
days.focus: Determination can persist alongside a real physical limit.
days.context: Kehonka has joined a wild flock for the night. When morning comes, he tries to keep pace with their flight. This night reaches the end of the story.
days.contentNote: The story ends with a fox killing Kehonka, told in a few sentences.

excerpt.locator: The Homesickness of Kehonka; contiguous excerpt, 5 source blocks; opens “When the signal-cry came, and the flock took flight, Kehonka rose with …”; closes “… carrying, and trotted off with it into the darkness of the woods.”.

questions.prompt: Why does joining the flock at dawn fail to solve Kehonka’s problem?
facilitatorNotes: He cannot match its speed while balancing unequal wings, despite intense effort.
evidence: he soon saw that this speed of theirs was beyond him

questions.prompt: How does he keep moving after he falls into the river?
facilitatorNotes: The tide carries him north; then he swims, walks and tries shorter flights. List changes in their order.
evidence: he began to swim in the same direction

questions.prompt: Why does he leave the main river and later the smaller stream?
facilitatorNotes: Their courses no longer carry him toward his goal. Direction matters more to him than the easiest path.
evidence: because its direction failed him

questions.prompt: Why does Kehonka fail to notice the danger in the woods?
facilitatorNotes: The wind carries the fox’s smell away from him, and his longing for the passing flock absorbs every sense: homesickness, the story’s title, causes his death. Some readers may see the fox’s name, “the discourager of quests”, as grimly ironic.
evidence: every sense was now numb in the presence of his great desire

days.title: In Panoply of Spears — excerpt: the bee-tree and the bear
days.challenge: Explain how a difference in defence can outweigh a difference in size.
days.focus: An accidental encounter protects the bees.
days.context: A maple tree shelters a bee colony and a sleeping porcupine. A bear returns to a place he remembers.
days.contentNote: The ending reports that the bear is later killed in a trap.

excerpt.locator: In Panoply of Spears; contiguous excerpt, 9 source blocks; opens “There was a pleasant humming all about the bee-tree, where it stood …”; closes “… in the bee-tree were left to possess their honeyed commonwealth in peace.”.

questions.prompt: Why might a distant observer mistake the porcupine for a nest?
facilitatorNotes: It is a still rounded shape high in the branches. Close details reveal paws and a hidden head.
evidence: taken for a big bird’s-nest

questions.prompt: Why does the bear try again after failing two years earlier?
facilitatorNotes: He hopes decay has weakened the wood around the honey. Memory connects his earlier failure with his present plan.
evidence: wait for the natural processes of decay to weaken the walls

questions.prompt: Does the porcupine set out to defend the bees?
facilitatorNotes: No. It wants to leave the tree; protection is an accidental result.
evidence: His present whim was to descend the bee-tree

questions.prompt: Why does the much larger bear give way?
facilitatorNotes: It recognises the painful risk of the quills, especially to nose and paws. Weight alone does not settle the encounter.
evidence: the bear stopped; and the porcupine came on

days.title: In Panoply of Spears — excerpt: passing through the woods
days.challenge: Compare reactions by asking what each animal has reason to fear.
days.focus: Appearance alone does not determine danger.
days.context: The porcupine leaves the bee-tree and heads toward an oat-field. Other animals respond to it in very different ways.
days.contentNote: Roberts gives the animals human-like judgments and feelings.

excerpt.locator: In Panoply of Spears; contiguous excerpt, 4 source blocks; opens “Soon after the bear had left the knoll, the porcupine appeared to …”; closes “… a mile around. The porcupine, uncurling, grunted scornfully and resumed his journey.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the porcupine travel more noisily and openly than other animals?
facilitatorNotes: Its quills make it feel protected; it does not need their constant concealment.
evidence: He did not care who knew of his coming

questions.prompt: Why does the mouse ignore the porcupine but flee the weasel?
facilitatorNotes: The porcupine does not hunt mice; the weasel does. The mouse’s response is based on the kind of threat.
evidence: had no concern for wood-mice

questions.prompt: How does the lynx’s angry scream work against its own purpose?
facilitatorNotes: It warns possible prey nearby and forces it to seek a new hunting place.
evidence: had warned all the coverts for a quarter of a mile around

days.title: In Panoply of Spears — excerpt: the oat-field and the yellow dog
days.challenge: Explain a sequence of physical actions from a dense description.
days.focus: An animal’s slow movement does not mean a lack of resourcefulness.
days.context: The porcupine reaches a partly abandoned clearing where a farmer still grows grain. Read once with help for the old landscape words, then reread the solution aloud.
days.contentNote: The farmer’s dog is struck by quills; the farmer pulls them out with his teeth and hunts the porcupine with a fence-stake but does not find it.

excerpt.locator: In Panoply of Spears; contiguous excerpt, 9 source blocks; opens “Very still, and lonely and bright the clearing lay in the flooding …”; closes “… he produced from his hip-pocket, and strode away up the grassy wood-road.”.

questions.prompt: Why has the clearing remained in use though its cabin is ruined?
facilitatorNotes: The soil is fertile enough for crops; the farmer lives elsewhere.
evidence: its fertile soil had saved it from being forgotten

questions.prompt: How can a watcher tell where the hidden porcupine is moving?
facilitatorNotes: The tops of the oats sway even though its body is concealed.
evidence: the swaying and commotion among the oat-tops

questions.prompt: How does the porcupine bring many oat-tops within reach at once?
facilitatorNotes: It circles while leaning inward until the tops gather into a bunch, then pulls the sheaf down. Invite a gesture or simple sketch.
evidence: the tops of the grain lay together in a convenient bunch

questions.prompt: Why does the yellow dog dare to attack here when he would leave a porcupine alone in the woods?
facilitatorNotes: He is guarding his master’s field, expects his master’s help, and has long wanted to kill a porcupine. The quills on the tail end the attack.
evidence: But in his master’s oat-field, that was a different matter.

days.title: In Panoply of Spears — excerpt: leave it alone
days.challenge: Separate a compassionate reason from a mistaken factual belief.
days.focus: A sound choice can be supported by both a good reason and a false one.
days.context: After driving off the farmer’s dog, the porcupine has hidden in a hole in the stone wall. Two children returning from school notice it. Alternate dialogue voices, then reread the sister’s last reason.
days.contentNote: The sister repeats the old belief that porcupines throw quills; they do not (see https://www.nps.gov/articles/acadia-porcupines.htm). The children’s speech is Roberts’s rendering of rural dialect.

excerpt.locator: In Panoply of Spears; contiguous excerpt, 10 source blocks; opens “For perhaps half an hour the porcupine dozed in the hole among …”; closes “… beyond the clearing, and the porcupine was left untroubled in his sovereignty.”.

questions.prompt: How does the sister act when her brother first wants to attack?
facilitatorNotes: She catches his arm and restrains him; she does more than express disapproval.
evidence: his sister clutched him by the arm

questions.prompt: Which of her reasons would remain sound even if the porcupine could not throw quills?
facilitatorNotes: It is harming no one and minding its own business. That reason supports leaving wildlife alone independently of the false belief.
evidence: He ain’t a-hurtin’ us

questions.prompt: Why does Jimmy put down his dinner-pail?
facilitatorNotes: He is preparing to throw a stone. The small action shows that his wish to attack has returned.
evidence: set down the tin dinner-pail, and picked up a stone

days.title: In Panoply of Spears — excerpt: a companion and a winter den
days.challenge: Trace a season and a partnership through food, shelter and changes in plants.
days.focus: Ordinary resources can be enough for survival.
days.context: In autumn, the porcupine eats lily pads beside a forest lake. Another porcupine approaches his narrow ledge. Read the short encounter twice, watching for its change in direction.
days.contentNote: Winter hunger and other animals’ hunting are mentioned.

excerpt.locator: In Panoply of Spears; contiguous excerpt, 7 source blocks; opens “That autumn, late one moonlight night, the porcupine was down by a …”; closes “… a porcupine baby was born in the snug den among the rocks.”.

questions.prompt: What makes a fight seem likely at first?
facilitatorNotes: The first porcupine bristles, gnashes its teeth and advances against the newcomer.
evidence: advanced to repel the intruder

questions.prompt: What details replace the expected conflict?
facilitatorNotes: They touch noses and make sounds together, then leave side by side.
evidence: the expected conflict was by some sudden agreement omitted

questions.prompt: What makes an old wooden container an unexpected feast?
facilitatorNotes: It has absorbed salt brine from pork, so they enjoy gnawing the flavoured wood.
evidence: The wood, saturated with brine, was delicious

questions.prompt: How does the final paragraph show that spring has arrived without relying only on its name?
facilitatorNotes: Running water, swelling buds, flowers and bright new growth supply visible and audible signs. Select two and explain them.
evidence: the maples crimsoned with their misty blooms

days.title: In Panoply of Spears — ending: the weasel in the den
days.challenge: Follow a fast fight by tracking who blocks the den’s door and where each animal moves.
days.focus: The porcupine’s armour, the “panoply of spears” of the title, decides the story’s ending.
days.context: In spring a baby porcupine has been born in the den. Unusually, the father has stayed with his mate and young.
days.contentNote: A weasel kills the three-day-old porcupine, and the father’s quills kill the weasel. Roberts calls the weasel an “assassin” and “murderer”; those moral labels are his narrator’s.

excerpt.locator: In Panoply of Spears; contiguous excerpt, 8 source blocks; opens “It was an astonishingly big baby,—the biggest, in proportion to the size …”; closes “… on the knoll, he found himself a new home, small and solitary.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the weasel believe the den is safe to enter?
facilitatorNotes: He smelled the mother’s trail leading away and assumed the male had left, as males usually do. The opening detail that this father stayed in the den makes the mistake fatal.
evidence: the prowler took it for granted that he had followed the usage of his kind
kept his place contentedly in the den

questions.prompt: How does the title, “In Panoply of Spears”, explain how the weasel is beaten, even though the porcupine first fights with his teeth?
facilitatorNotes: A panoply is a full suit of armour. The weasel is thrown onto the raised quills, and the tail-slap adds more; the porcupine “scorned his customary tactics”, yet his armour still decides the fight.
evidence: full upon the stiffly erected spears of the porcupine’s back

questions.prompt: Why does the porcupine leave the den at the end?
facilitatorNotes: With the baby dead, his reason to stay is gone and he returns to the solitary life of his kind. Accept readings that stress grief or that stress Roberts’s idea of instinct, with evidence from the last paragraph.
evidence: the time of partings had come
he would never find another like it!

days.title: Sea Sunset
days.challenge: Follow one extended comparison through a whole poem.
days.focus: A sunset becoming an unreachable city.
days.context: Imagine the cloud shapes first, then reread to notice what is real and what is wished for.

excerpt.locator: Sea Sunset; complete work, 4 source blocks; opens “A gallant city has been builded far In the pied heaven, Bannered …”; closes “… come shoreward roaming, And the dim west has only gray and gloaming.”.

blocks.text:
A gallant city has been builded far
In the pied heaven,
Bannered with crimson, sentinelled by star
Of crystal even;
Around a harbor of the twilight glowing,
With jubilant waves about its gateways flowing.

A city of the Land of Lost Delight
On seas enchanted,
Presently to be lost in mist moon-white
And music-haunted;
Given but briefly to our raptured vision,
With all its opal towers and shrines elysian.

Had we some mystic boat with pearly oar
And wizard pilot,
To guide us safely by the siren shore
And cloudy islet,
We might embark and reach that shining portal
Beyond which linger dreams and joys immortal.

But we may only gaze with longing eyes
On those far, sparkling
Palaces in the fairy-peopled skies,
O'er waters darkling,
Until the winds of night come shoreward roaming,
And the dim west has only gray and gloaming.

questions.prompt: What features make the sky look like a city?
facilitatorNotes: Banners, gateways, towers, shrines, and palaces turn colored clouds into architecture.
evidence: With all its opal towers and shrines elysian.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker imagine a special boat and pilot?
facilitatorNotes: An ordinary boat cannot reach a city made of sunset clouds; the imagined voyage needs magic.
evidence: Had we some mystic boat with pearly oar

questions.prompt: What remains when the vision ends?
facilitatorNotes: The west becomes gray and dusky. The loss makes the brief colored vision more precious.
evidence: the dim west has only gray and gloaming.

days.title: The Chipmunk — burrow and stripes (excerpt)
days.challenge: Compare a qualified claim with a visible description.
days.focus: A hidden home and a body that blends into its surroundings.
days.context: This historical passage moves from a chipmunk’s burrow to its stripes and tail. “Presumably” signals an inference.

excerpt.locator: The Chipmunk — burrow and stripes (excerpt); contiguous excerpt, 2 source blocks; opens “The chipmunk is a good home builder and carries off, presumably in …”; closes “… earth and would be an incubus instead of a thing of beauty.”.

questions.prompt: Which word shows that Comstock is not certain how soil is carried away?
facilitatorNotes: “Presumably” marks a proposed explanation rather than something she reports watching here.
evidence: presumably in its cheek pouches

questions.prompt: What is the use of a back entrance to the burrow?
facilitatorNotes: It supplies a way to escape if needed; the passage presents the home as practical shelter.
evidence: so that in case of necessity, the inmate can escape.

questions.prompt: Why might a bushy tree-squirrel tail be inconvenient underground?
facilitatorNotes: It could collect earth; the writer contrasts life in trees with life in a burrow.
evidence: a bushy tail would soon be loaded with earth

days.title: A Cradle Song (Songs of Innocence)
days.challenge: Trace repeated gentle commands as the poem moves toward religious reflection.
days.focus: A parent’s care expressed as a lullaby.
days.context: Read slowly, with soft stresses on “sweet” and “sleep.” The second half connects a baby with the Christian image of Jesus as an infant.
days.contentNote: This poem expresses the author’s Christian belief. Discuss that viewpoint without asking readers to share it.

excerpt.locator: A Cradle Song (Songs of Innocence); complete work, 8 source blocks; opens “Sweet dreams, form a shade O’er my lovely infant’s head! Sweet dreams …”; closes “… Infant smiles are His own smiles; Heaven and earth to peace beguiles.”.

questions.prompt: What kind of shelter do the opening dreams seem to make?
facilitatorNotes: They form a shade over the infant, as if dreams could protect the sleeping child.
evidence: Sweet dreams, form a shade

questions.prompt: How do the repeated words help the poem sound like something sung beside a cradle?
facilitatorNotes: Sweet and sleep recur in short lines; their steady, soothing return matters more than a fast plot.
evidence: Sleep, sleep, happy child!

questions.prompt: How does the poem’s circle of concern grow beyond this one child?
facilitatorNotes: It moves from the mother’s baby to the religious figure who weeps for “me,” “thee,” and “all.”
evidence: Wept for me, for thee, for all,

days.title: Song of the Sea-Wind
days.challenge: Identify an unusual first-person speaker and keep its changing moods separate.
days.focus: Freedom that can be playful or frightening.
days.context: The wind speaks in this poem. Read its verbs aloud and notice the difference between calm and storm.

excerpt.locator: Song of the Sea-Wind; complete work, 3 source blocks; opens “When the sun sets over the long blue wave I spring from …”; closes “… the land is a hindered thing But the ocean wind is free!”.

blocks.text:
When the sun sets over the long blue wave
I spring from my couch of rest,
And I hurtle and boom over leagues of foam
That toss in the weltering west,
I pipe a hymn to the headlands high,
My comrades forevermore,
And I chase the tricksy curls of foam
O'er the glimmering sandy shore.

The moon is my friend on clear, white nights
When I ripple her silver way,
And whistle blithely about the rocks
Like an elfin thing at play;
But anon I ravin with cloud and mist
And wail 'neath a curdled sky,
When the reef snarls yon like a questing beast,
And the frightened ships go by.

I scatter the dawn across the sea
Like wine of amber flung
From a crystal goblet all far and fine
Where the morning star is hung;
I blow from east and I blow from west
Wherever my longing be—
The wind of the land is a hindered thing
But the ocean wind is free!

questions.prompt: Who is speaking, and what does the speaker chase along the shore?
facilitatorNotes: The sea-wind speaks and chases curls of foam. The title and last line help establish the speaker.
evidence: I chase the tricksy curls of foam

questions.prompt: What makes the middle stanza less playful?
facilitatorNotes: Cloud, mist, a curdled sky, a snarling reef, and frightened ships turn the wind threatening.
evidence: When the reef snarls yon like a questing beast,

questions.prompt: Why does the ending contrast the land wind with the ocean wind?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker boasts of open movement over the sea, describing land wind as hindered. This is the wind’s poetic claim.
evidence: The wind of the land is a hindered thing

days.title: The Sunflower — many flowers working together (excerpt)
days.challenge: Use the explanation to revise the everyday meaning of one flower.
days.focus: Cooperation as an analogy for a composite flower-head.
days.context: “Compositæ” names a plant family. Adult and child can reread the terms ray-flower, disk-flower, and floret together.
days.contentNote: Comstock wrote this handbook for teachers; her directions to the class are part of the 1911 text.

excerpt.locator: The Sunflower — many flowers working together (excerpt); contiguous excerpt, 3 source blocks; opens “Many of the most beautiful of the autumn flowers belong to the …”; closes “… pupils understand this fact it is necessary to study the individual florets.”.

questions.prompt: Why can one sunflower head be described as many flowers?
facilitatorNotes: The head holds many individual florets arranged together, rather than being only one flower.
evidence: many flowers associated to form a single flower-head.

questions.prompt: How does the author distinguish the jobs of ray-flowers and disk-flowers?
facilitatorNotes: The bright outer rays attract insects; the central disk flowers handle pollination and seed production.
evidence: hold out bright pennants to attract the attention of insects;

questions.prompt: Why does Comstock choose a large garden sunflower for explaining this arrangement?
facilitatorNotes: Its large florets are easier to see, like parts enlarged in a wax model.
evidence: Its florets are so large that it is like a great wax model.

days.title: The Book of Beasts, excerpt 1: A child becomes king
days.challenge: Alternate reading the short dialogue turns while an adult supports the longer ceremonial description.
days.focus: How ordinary childhood habits make a royal event comic.
days.context: Lionel is playing at home when two officials arrive with unexpected news. Read the narrator’s royal grandeur alongside ordinary nursery details.
days.contentNote: The narrator makes a dated generalization about girls and clothes; it is a stereotype, not a fact. A distant ancestor’s death is mentioned.

excerpt.locator: I. The Book of Beasts; contiguous excerpt, 22 source blocks; opens “He happened to be building a Palace when the news came, and …”; closes “… and real tea, and as many cups of it as you liked.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Lionel ask when he should be fetched, as if becoming king were a visit?
facilitatorNotes: He understands the unfamiliar event through visits to tea. His familiar questions reveal how young and unprepared he is.
evidence: said Lionel, who had often been out to tea.

questions.prompt: How does Lionel’s final exchange with Nurse differ from his complaints while she washes him?
facilitatorNotes: He changes from resisting her care to thanking and kissing her. Invite readers to notice affection beneath the comic impatience.
evidence: Thank you for washing me. I wish I'd let you do the other ear.

questions.prompt: What is surprising about the people saving for a crown before Lionel can be king?
facilitatorNotes: A grand monarchy depends on small weekly payments and an unpaid bill. The practical money details make the ceremony less lofty and more like everyday shopping.
evidence: the crown must be paid for by the people.

days.title: The Book of Beasts, excerpt 2: Pictures take flight
days.challenge: Track several speakers and distinguish a warning from evidence that the warning is justified.
days.focus: The first signs of magic and contrasting responses to curiosity.
days.context: After his coronation, Lionel asks for a book. The officials have warned him that his ancestor’s books may be unusual.
days.contentNote: An adult shakes Lionel and calls him naughty.

excerpt.locator: I. The Book of Beasts; contiguous excerpt, 30 source blocks; opens “After tea Lionel said: "I think I should like a book. Will …”; closes “… noughts and crosses while the Chancellor went to add up his accounts.”.

questions.prompt: Why is Lionel delighted when he learns that the library belongs to him?
facilitatorNotes: He values the chance to read, not merely owning royal objects. His repeated declaration makes his pleasure unmistakable.
evidence: I love to read. I am so glad I learned to read.

questions.prompt: Which movement first proves the Butterfly is more than a beautiful painting?
facilitatorNotes: Its wings move and it leaves the book through the window. Ask readers to distinguish looking lifelike from actually acting alive.
evidence: flew up and out of the window.

questions.prompt: Does Lionel’s claim that he has done no harm settle the officials’ concern?
facilitatorNotes: No: he has observed two harmless creatures, but does not know what later pages contain. Readers may defend his curiosity while recognizing the uncertainty.
evidence: How do you know what might have been on the next page

days.title: The Book of Beasts, excerpt 3: A law cannot stop a dragon
days.challenge: Follow cause and consequence across several days; have an adult read the longer satirical paragraphs. For this longer scene, the adult reads the source aloud and the child rereads only a chosen short quotation.
days.focus: How public praise and royal power fail to repair a concrete mistake.
days.context: Lionel cannot stop thinking about the forbidden book. The earlier Butterfly and Blue Bird escaped harmlessly; he does not yet know the next creature’s effect.
days.contentNote: Fantasy peril: a dragon swallows groups of people, including an orphanage; later in the story they return unharmed. Adults slap and shame Lionel. These actions are presented for critical discussion.

excerpt.locator: I. The Book of Beasts; contiguous excerpt, 22 source blocks; opens “But when Lionel was in bed he could not sleep for thinking …”; closes “… was his duty to try and do something. The question was, what?”.

questions.prompt: Why does Lionel feel especially guilty when the Dragon escapes?
facilitatorNotes: He remembers that the people saved to buy his crown, so the danger feels like a betrayal of their kindness as well as disobedience.
evidence: And they had been saving up so long to buy him a crown, and everything!

questions.prompt: Why is the statement that a crowned Lionel cannot make a mistake funny or doubtful here?
facilitatorNotes: Readers have just witnessed his mistake. The narrator exposes a gap between the ceremony of authority and actual good judgment.
evidence: everything he said was right, and that he couldn't possibly make a mistake.

questions.prompt: What change in Lionel’s thinking closes this part?
facilitatorNotes: Instead of relying on popular laws or forgiveness, he decides he has a duty to act. He does not yet have a solution, which makes the ending a problem to carry forward.
evidence: he felt that it was his duty to try and do something.

days.title: The Book of Beasts, excerpt 4: An unexpected ally
days.challenge: Compare a creature’s reputation with its actions, then notice how descriptive language changes for the Hippogriff. For this longer scene, the adult reads the source aloud and the child rereads only a chosen short quotation.
days.focus: The difference between assuming a helper will be fierce and recognizing actual help.
days.context: The dragon has caused damage, and Lionel wants a creature that can stop it. The escaped Blue Bird and Butterfly remind him that the book also holds kindly beings.
days.contentNote: Fantasy animals are eaten, and a battle is described through noise and tufts of fur; the tale later restores the swallowed creatures. The text includes a threatening blood-drinking description.

excerpt.locator: I. The Book of Beasts; contiguous excerpt, 16 source blocks; opens “The Blue Bird that had come out of the book used to …”; closes “… Rocking Horse." And the Blue Bird's song was very loud and sweet.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Lionel think opening the book again could help rather than only cause another problem?
facilitatorNotes: He uses the gentle Bird and Butterfly as counterexamples: not every creature from the book is like the Dragon.
evidence: all the creatures in The Book of Beasts could not be wicked

questions.prompt: How does the Manticora fail to match the Chancellor’s account?
facilitatorNotes: The Chancellor calls it a sworn enemy of dragons, but it runs away and hides. A reputation or species description does not guarantee this creature’s behavior.
evidence: it put its tail between its legs and fairly ran away.

questions.prompt: What makes the Hippogriff seem promising before it has fought or rescued anyone?
facilitatorNotes: Its friendly sounds, gentle touch, and kind eyes establish trust. Readers may also connect it to Lionel’s lost rocking horse.
evidence: the softest, kindest eyes in the world

days.title: The Book of Beasts, excerpt 5: The only tree
days.challenge: Reconstruct the plan from the setting, time of day, and object placement; let the child retell the solution before rereading.
days.focus: A rescue achieved through observation rather than strength.
days.context: Lionel rides the winged Hippogriff away with the book. He knows the Dragon must rest in shade at noon, and he chooses where the chase will end.
days.contentNote: Fantasy danger resolves here: people and animals swallowed earlier return unharmed.

excerpt.locator: I. The Book of Beasts; contiguous excerpt, 19 source blocks; opens “And when the Dragon saw them start, he turned and flew after …”; closes “… the lilies and roses of the Palace garden to this very day.”.

questions.prompt: Why is the treeless Pebbly Waste essential to Lionel’s plan?
facilitatorNotes: At noon the Dragon needs shade, and the painted palm becomes its only available tree. The setting forces the creature back into its picture.
evidence: there was not a tree for a hundred miles.

questions.prompt: What does Lionel do immediately after the Dragon enters the book, and why does the timing matter?
facilitatorNotes: He closes and clasps it before the creature can escape again. The action turns the temporary retreat into a successful capture.
evidence: shut the book with a bang.

questions.prompt: How does the ending repair more than the immediate danger?
facilitatorNotes: The swallowed people, animals, and rocking horse return, and the friendly Hippogriff stays with Lionel. Accept answers that name specific restorations and explain their effect.
evidence: everyone who had been eaten by the Dragon.

days.title: The Dragon Tamers, excerpt 1: A noise below the forge
days.challenge: Read the long opening with adult support, then listen for the mismatch between what the adults say and what they fear. For this longer scene, the adult reads the source aloud and the child rereads only a chosen short quotation.
days.focus: How setting and repeated sounds build suspense.
days.context: A new story begins with a poor blacksmith named John, his exhausted wife, and their baby living in the remains of a castle.
days.contentNote: The ruined dungeon’s history includes cruel treatment of prisoners. The family experiences poverty and exhaustion. These are fictional circumstances, not a claim that poor families are at fault.

excerpt.locator: VI. The Dragon Tamers; contiguous excerpt, 16 source blocks; opens “There was once an old, old castle—it was so old that its …”; closes “… It was quite full, and what it was full of was Dragon.”.

questions.prompt: How does the mayor’s forge help explain why John receives so little work?
facilitatorNotes: It has many workers and modern equipment and attracts local customers; John mostly gets strangers. Ask readers to connect resources and opportunity, not blame his effort.
evidence: the townspeople, whenever they wanted a horse shod or a shaft mended, went to the mayor.

questions.prompt: Why do the blacksmith’s hammering and his wife’s singing become louder?
facilitatorNotes: They are trying to cover or deny the frightening sound below them. Their actions reveal fear despite their words.
evidence: the more they tried not to hear it, the more they had to.

questions.prompt: How does the wife know the hammer is not really needed to break coal?
facilitatorNotes: She brought home coal dust, which contains no large lumps to break. This detail lets readers see through John’s excuse.
evidence: knew that it was all coal dust.

days.title: The Dragon Tamers, excerpt 2: A customer with loose rivets
days.challenge: Follow the changing bargain and infer the purpose of John’s polite language. For this longer scene, the adult reads the source aloud and the child rereads only a chosen short quotation.
days.focus: Craft knowledge and quick thinking under pressure.
days.context: John has found a dragon in his dungeon. The dragon’s damaged wing creates an opening for the blacksmith’s skill and a dangerous bargain.
days.contentNote: A dragon threatens to eat people, and a baby is placed near it during a risky bargain.

excerpt.locator: VI. The Dragon Tamers; contiguous excerpt, 44 source blocks; opens “"It must have come up those nasty broken steps from goodness knows …”; closes “… laughing and crowing with pleasure at the very large purr of it.”.

questions.prompt: What changes when John recognizes the dragon’s loose metal plates?
facilitatorNotes: His professional knowledge gives him something he can understand and do; he becomes less helpless even though the danger remains.
evidence: All the blacksmith welled up in John's heart, and he felt more at ease.

questions.prompt: How does John make fastening the dragon sound like normal workshop practice?
facilitatorNotes: He compares it with tying up a horse and stresses accidental injury. His argument protects him while allowing the dragon to preserve its dignity.
evidence: We always fasten a horse up

questions.prompt: Why does John warn that babies are poison to dragons?
facilitatorNotes: He wants to discourage the dragon from eating the baby. The story gives no independent proof of this claim; treat it as a protective tactic in the bargain.
evidence: Babies are poison to dragons

days.title: The Dragon Tamers, excerpt 3: Who receives the reward?
days.challenge: Track who takes action and who receives credit; an adult can explain the old money words without calculating them. For this longer scene, the adult reads the source aloud and the child rereads only a chosen short quotation.
days.focus: Satire of public praise that does not match actual service.
days.context: John seeks help while his baby remains with the chained dragon. Later, the town celebrates its rescue and raises money supposedly in gratitude.
days.contentNote: Adults discuss possible harm to a baby; the mother retrieves the child safely. The mayor’s indifference is a subject for criticism.

excerpt.locator: VI. The Dragon Tamers; contiguous excerpt, 29 source blocks; opens “John ran as hard as he could into the town, and found …”; closes “… fire to look at him by. And they grew older and wiser.”.

questions.prompt: What does the mayor offer when John asks for practical help with the baby?
facilitatorNotes: He offers a comforting-sounding story about a good cause rather than assistance. Readers should notice how this avoids responsibility.
evidence: your baby perished in a good cause.

questions.prompt: How is the baby finally brought upstairs safely?
facilitatorNotes: The dragon becomes exhausted by the crying and asks the mother to take the baby. The parents understand a need the officials ignore.
evidence: Then I wish you'd take this one, and let me get some sleep

questions.prompt: Why is the list of the three celebratory poems unfair?
facilitatorNotes: They praise the mayor, corporation, and poet rather than the blacksmith who secured the dragon. The spending similarly rewards officials.
evidence: The first poem dealt with the noble conduct of the mayor

days.title: The Dragon Tamers, excerpt 4: The children bargain
days.challenge: Connect a remembered injustice with Johnnie’s new negotiation and identify the changing threats.
days.focus: How memory and community support alter a bargain.
days.context: Years have passed. Johnnie, the former baby, and Tina know the captive dragon. A new threat gives them an idea, but the mayor again resists rewarding the real helpers.
days.contentNote: A giant and dragon fight in non-graphic fantasy, and the dragon threatens the town. The giant is described with dated, unkind language about disability.

excerpt.locator: VI. The Dragon Tamers; contiguous excerpt, 30 source blocks; opens “At last one day the mayor and corporation, hunting the hare in …”; closes “"Oh, yes," said the dragon, "it's very dull here."”.

questions.prompt: Why do Johnnie and Tina think the dragon might help with the giant?
facilitatorNotes: They know it is trapped and powerful; freedom gives it a reason to act. Its claim to favor peace should be compared with what it then does.
evidence: You let me out, and you'll see.

questions.prompt: Why does Johnnie refuse to trust another promise from the mayor?
facilitatorNotes: He remembers how his father’s earlier rescue brought no promised money. His suspicion rests on evidence from the earlier episode.
evidence: Look how you treated my father when he chained up the dragon.

questions.prompt: What makes the new promise of a reward different from the mayor’s offer?
facilitatorNotes: The townspeople themselves promise to replace the mayor with Johnnie. Their public involvement creates a different source of authority.
evidence: they would turn out the mayor and let Johnnie be mayor in his place.

days.title: The Dragon Tamers, closing excerpt: A change of heart
days.challenge: Follow the shift from trickster victory to sympathy and recognize the invented explanation of cats.
days.focus: A comic origin story that complicates who deserves kindness.
days.context: Johnnie and Tina have tricked the dragon into being chained again by inventing a giant who eats wild dragons. The town celebrates; this closing scene considers the captive’s future.
days.contentNote: Threats of being eaten are part of Nesbit’s comic fantasy.

excerpt.locator: VI. The Dragon Tamers; contiguous excerpt, 12 source blocks; opens “This was all very well for Johnnie and Tina; but if you …”; closes “… of dragons. And then there would be all the bother over again.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the dragon first try the children’s bread and milk?
facilitatorNotes: It feels faint after crying and notices the tub left behind. Its immediate hunger leads to an unexpected liking, rather than another violent demand.
evidence: perhaps I should like it too

questions.prompt: How do Johnnie and Tina show that they believe the dragon has changed?
facilitatorNotes: They release it; their wedding-day happiness makes them willing to trust it after its years of gentler behavior. The story moves from tricking an enemy to trusting a friend, and the dragon responds with a gift.
evidence: So they loosened the chains

questions.prompt: Which final changes turn this story into a playful explanation of where cats came from?
facilitatorNotes: The armor and wings fall away, fur grows, and claws remain. The impossible transformation signals a made-up origin tale rather than factual natural history.
evidence: he was the beginning of all cats.

days.title: The Deliverers of Their Country, excerpt 1: A very small discovery
days.challenge: Share the scientific vocabulary; let the child read Effie’s short observations and compare them with the adults’ labels.
days.focus: Different ways of recognizing the same creature.
days.context: Effie brings home something unusual in her eye. Her father and a professor study it, but the discoveries soon outgrow their collecting.
days.contentNote: A dog is bitten and a worker is burned by Nesbit’s dragons.

excerpt.locator: III. The Deliverers of Their Country; contiguous excerpt, 17 source blocks; opens “It all began with Effie's getting something in her eye. It hurt …”; closes “… the wings were a pale, half-transparent yellow, like the gear-boxes on bicycles.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Effie ask for payment for the specimen?
facilitatorNotes: She sees herself as its finder and carrier, and her discomfort as work that deserves recognition. Her practical view contrasts with her father’s scientific excitement.
evidence: I took great care of it inside my eye

questions.prompt: How does the professor turn discovery into a competition?
facilitatorNotes: He buys Harry’s creature quickly and calls it finer than the doctor’s. That comparison suggests rivalry as well as curiosity.
evidence: and finer than yours, Doctor.

questions.prompt: What makes Effie’s name for the animal different from the newspapers’ name?
facilitatorNotes: She recognizes a dragon from a story; newspapers insist on winged lizards because they refuse to accept fairy-tale creatures. The narrator explicitly supports Effie.
evidence: And Effie was right.

days.title: The Deliverers of Their Country, excerpt 2: Too many dragons
days.challenge: Keep track of how the repeated sentence changes the effect of each attempted solution.
days.focus: Repetition, failed remedies, and the appeal of adventure.
days.context: The once-rare dragons now fill the country. This excerpt follows the failure of official remedies and the effects on children’s ordinary lives.
days.contentNote: Fantasy danger includes creatures carrying off people and animals and mass killing of dragons. Harry’s comment about girls is a stereotype. Poison handling in the fantasy is not a real-world activity.

excerpt.locator: III. The Deliverers of Their Country; contiguous excerpt, 10 source blocks; opens “They breathed fire and smoke, as all proper dragons must, but still …”; closes “… to go out. Only they did not like to disobey their mother.”.

questions.prompt: Why do the smaller dragons cause trouble even when people avoid the large ones?
facilitatorNotes: They hide in ordinary objects and places, such as soap, butter, baskets, and beds. Size does not measure the amount of disruption.
evidence: The ones as big as earwigs got in the soap

questions.prompt: What does the repeated statement about the number of dragons do to the descriptions of official action?
facilitatorNotes: Each remedy sounds energetic, but the refrain shows no improvement. It builds frustration and makes another kind of solution necessary.
evidence: And yet there seemed to be more dragons than ever.

questions.prompt: Why do the children first enjoy their changed schedule and then tire of it?
facilitatorNotes: Staying up all night seems novel, but it denies them sunshine and outdoor play. Ask for the specific freedoms they miss.
evidence: They wanted to see the flowers and trees growing in the fields

days.title: The Deliverers of Their Country, excerpt 3: Waking a champion
days.challenge: Read the dialogue by roles; distinguish the children’s first interpretation from the usefulness of a later clue.
days.focus: Why an old solution may not fit a new problem.
days.context: Effie and Harry leave in daylight to seek St. George. The country’s many dragons require more than the single battle they know from a legend.
days.contentNote: Dragons threaten the children, and Harry dismisses Effie’s fear.

excerpt.locator: III. The Deliverers of Their Country; contiguous excerpt, 24 source blocks; opens “So the next afternoon, quite early, long before the beams of sunset …”; closes “… back into his marble and was fast asleep again in a moment.”.

questions.prompt: What finally wakes St. George after Harry’s attempts fail?
facilitatorNotes: Effie’s affectionate plea and kiss wake him. Her gentler approach succeeds where calling and shaking do not.
evidence: she kissed the marble face

questions.prompt: Why does St. George refuse to fight the dragons himself?
facilitatorNotes: He fought one dragon at a time, whereas the country now has a multitude. His old method does not fit the scale of the problem.
evidence: one man one dragon, was my motto.

questions.prompt: Why is the question about the weather more useful than Harry thinks?
facilitatorNotes: It connects the dragons’ survival to heat and points toward cold and water as a solution. Effie answers patiently and learns the clue.
evidence: dragons can't stand wet and cold

days.title: The Deliverers of Their Country, excerpt 4: The room of taps
days.challenge: Trace how an ordinary object and a remembered clue help the children make decisions. For this longer scene, the adult reads the source aloud and the child rereads only a chosen short quotation.
days.focus: A frightening detour becomes the route to a solution.
days.context: St. George has mentioned a room of weather taps. The children protect the sleeping champion, then an unwanted flight carries them toward the very place they need.
days.contentNote: A dragon carries the children away and threatens to eat them; they escape with a knife and poison.

excerpt.locator: III. The Deliverers of Their Country; contiguous excerpt, 18 source blocks; opens “"We shall never find the taps," said Harry. "I say, wouldn't it …”; closes “… was still broad daylight, and no dragons had gone to bed yet.”.

questions.prompt: What do the children give up when they protect St. George?
facilitatorNotes: They leave their own protective veil and poison with him. Their care for him makes their next danger more striking.
evidence: So she covered St. George with the veil

questions.prompt: How do the children escape when the knife cannot cut Harry’s coat?
facilitatorNotes: Effie cuts herself out of her sash, then helps Harry wriggle out of his sleeves. They adapt the plan instead of requiring the knife to do everything.
evidence: Harry managed to wriggle quietly out of his sleeves

questions.prompt: How does the looking glass change what the children know?
facilitatorNotes: They can see events far away, including their worried mother and the dragons throughout England. It will also let them observe the effects of the taps.
evidence: you could see everything that was going on in the world

days.title: The Deliverers of Their Country, excerpt 5: What the mirror shows
days.challenge: Follow a two-stage solution and compare the public ending with each family member’s response.
days.focus: Solving the remaining problem after an apparent victory.
days.context: The children have reached the controls of the weather. They can now test a solution and watch what happens throughout the country.
days.contentNote: Rain kills the fantasy dragons, whose bodies are washed away. The imagined weather controls are not a scientific explanation of climate.

excerpt.locator: III. The Deliverers of Their Country; contiguous excerpt, 21 source blocks; opens “Effie said, "Dragons do not like cold." And she tried to turn …”; closes “You must get him to show it to you!”.

questions.prompt: Why does killing the dragons not finish the children’s work?
facilitatorNotes: Their bodies remain everywhere, too many to bury and too wet to burn. Effie notices this practical problem before celebrating.
evidence: What can they do with such a lot of dead dragons?

questions.prompt: How do they discover what the rusty tap does?
facilitatorNotes: They clean its label, predict that Waste may remove the dragons, turn it, and watch the mirror. Their actions form an observation-and-test sequence inside the fantasy.
evidence: the label said "Waste."

questions.prompt: How do Mother’s and Father’s first responses reveal different concerns?
facilitatorNotes: Mother cares that her children are safe, even while scolding them; Father regrets losing a specimen. The contrast is comic but also points to different priorities.
evidence: I should have liked to preserve a specimen.

days.title: The Ice Dragon, excerpt 1: Lights beyond the garden
days.challenge: Notice two contrasting styles of description; an adult supports the old place names and celebration customs.
days.focus: The gap between naming a wonder and explaining it.
days.context: George and Jane are outside watching a fireworks celebration. From the garden fence they notice the Northern Lights and begin imagining a journey toward them.
days.contentNote: George makes dismissive comments about his sister. A comparison to Indigenous people reflects a stereotype common in Nesbit’s time.

excerpt.locator: IV. The Ice Dragon, or Do as You Are Told; contiguous excerpt, 28 source blocks; opens “They got up on the fence at the end of the garden …”; closes “… side. And then they stood still and held their breath with wonder.”.

questions.prompt: How do Jane and George describe the lights differently?
facilitatorNotes: Jane imagines fairies growing luminous trees; George uses the learned name Aurora Borealis. Both notice the same sight through different kinds of knowledge.
evidence: watering them with liquid light.

questions.prompt: Does knowing the name mean George can answer Jane’s questions about the lights?
facilitatorNotes: No. He admits he has not learned who lights them or why they are there. Naming and explaining are different achievements.
evidence: George had to own that he had not learned that.

questions.prompt: How does Jane use the distinction between lawn and grass to justify leaving?
facilitatorNotes: She treats the precise word as permission despite the obvious purpose of the instruction. Readers can identify this as a convenient interpretation.
evidence: They said the lawn

days.title: The Ice Dragon, excerpt 2: Two requests
days.challenge: Read the two encounters comparatively and identify the repeated question that changes each decision.
days.focus: Looking beyond a polite request to its intended use.
days.context: A magical ice slide carries George and Jane toward the North Pole. They cannot stop easily; twice a stranger calls to them and asks for a useful object.
days.contentNote: Adults plan to kill a bird and pin a moth; the children prevent both. Guns, fireworks, and sharp objects appear in dialogue.

excerpt.locator: IV. The Ice Dragon, or Do as You Are Told; contiguous excerpt, 25 source blocks; opens “It is very pleasant to slide and slide and slide on clear, …”; closes “… on, leaving him too, trying to go uphill towards the Crystal Palace.”.

questions.prompt: Why must the children tumble when someone calls for them to stop?
facilitatorNotes: The downhill slide keeps carrying them forward; falling is the only stopping method in this fantasy. That practical difficulty gives the repeated encounters their comic entrance.
evidence: because it is the only way to stop

questions.prompt: Why does George change his mind about lending the firework?
facilitatorNotes: Once he learns the sportsman wants to kill the grouse, he refuses. The purpose matters more than simply being helpful to the requester.
evidence: Ask him what he wants it for.

questions.prompt: How does Jane do more than refuse the collector’s request?
facilitatorNotes: She releases the moth while George explains. Her action directly protects the creature rather than merely withholding the pin.
evidence: Jane opened the blue folds of the butterfly net

days.title: The Ice Dragon, excerpt 3: Beauty and unease
days.challenge: Read the rich descriptions slowly and select one comparison to explain independently.
days.focus: How beauty and danger coexist in the same setting.
days.context: George and Jane have reached the glittering North Pole by an enchanted ice slide. George celebrates the discovery; Jane begins to worry about the return journey.
days.contentNote: Nesbit’s North Pole and its hostile sealskin dwarfs are her inventions.

excerpt.locator: IV. The Ice Dragon, or Do as You Are Told; contiguous excerpt, 20 source blocks; opens “"I daresay lots of people have gotten here," said Jane, dismally. "It's …”; closes “… are those fires for?" bellowed George—for Jane was crying louder and louder.”.

questions.prompt: Why is Jane less satisfied with arrival than George?
facilitatorNotes: She is already thinking about the return journey. He celebrates discovery, while she recognizes the practical problem the successful trip has created.
evidence: it's the getting back again.

questions.prompt: Which comparison helps you picture the dragon as something other than simply a monster?
facilitatorNotes: Accept a supported choice such as a jewel, rainbow glitter, or Prussian blue ice. These descriptions make it beautiful as well as threatening.
evidence: the dragon lay like an enormous jewel

questions.prompt: Why does George ask Jane to pretend to cry?
facilitatorNotes: The unfamiliar crying frightens the surrounding creatures. He hopes to use their surprise as protection while avoiding real tears freezing.
evidence: But pretend to howl—it frightens them.

days.title: The Ice Dragon, excerpt 4: Many small gifts
days.challenge: Connect an earlier choice with its later consequence, and separate a partial rescue from a complete one.
days.focus: Collective help and the limits of a helper’s understanding.
days.context: The sealskin creatures reveal a threatening plan and notice George’s fur cap. Help then arrives from a creature the children protected earlier.
days.contentNote: The children are tied up and threatened with being eaten. The hostile beings are fictional creatures made entirely of fur, not a representation of a real community.

excerpt.locator: IV. The Ice Dragon, or Do as You Are Told; contiguous excerpt, 25 source blocks; opens “"Those," shouted the dwarfs, coming a step nearer, "are the fires we …”; closes “… no one takes it from you. What more can you possibly want?"”.

questions.prompt: What do the creatures mean by saying their hearts resemble purses?
facilitatorNotes: They answer Jane literally by naming the material of their hearts. This misses her criticism of their lack of kindness and makes their response chillingly comic.
evidence: just like little fat sealskin purses

questions.prompt: How can the grouse cover two children without losing all its own feathers?
facilitatorNotes: Many birds each contribute a little. The amount becomes enough through cooperation, not through one bird sacrificing its entire covering.
evidence: every one of us can spare a little tuft

questions.prompt: Why are the children still uneasy after they become warm?
facilitatorNotes: They remain tied beside a dragon that may wake. The grouse understands warmth and shelter but overlooks the threat of being eaten.
evidence: What more can you possibly want?

days.title: The Ice Dragon, excerpt 5: The unlikely ride home
days.challenge: Distinguish what characters expect from what happens; let the child explain the last reversal before an adult rereads the ending.
days.focus: Unexpected help and a narrator who admits a gap in the explanation.
days.context: The rescued grouse supplied warm feathers, and moths defeated the hostile fur creatures who tied the children to the North Pole. The helpers have now left, but the dragon still lies beneath the children.
days.contentNote: Moths kill the hostile fur creatures, and the dragon eats two adults, without graphic bodily detail. The moth and aurora explanations are deliberate fantasy, not natural history.

excerpt.locator: IV. The Ice Dragon, or Do as You Are Told; contiguous excerpt, 19 source blocks; opens “And off they all fluttered, and the white grouse flew off, and …”; closes “… by moths—and motheaten things are of no use, even to light fires!”.

questions.prompt: Why does the departure of their helpers leave the children frightened despite the rescue?
facilitatorNotes: They are still bound beside a dragon in the dark and have no clear way home. Removing one threat has not solved every part of their situation.
evidence: We've no friends left to help us

questions.prompt: Why does the dragon wake when the fires go out, contrary to the creatures’ plan?
facilitatorNotes: It has become ice throughout; heat weakens it and cold restores it. The creatures misunderstand its nature, so their plan works backward.
evidence: the fires only made him feel as if he were going to die.

questions.prompt: How does the narrator answer the final question about the Northern Lights?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator admits not knowing who lit them again. This open gap resists treating the whole fantasy as a complete scientific explanation.
evidence: I am not too proud to own that there are some things I know nothing about

days.title: The Gulls
days.challenge: Compare three numbered scenes using the repeated time clues.
days.focus: A day told through the presence and absence of birds.
days.context: Try an independent first reading of the three short parts; ask a partner about unfamiliar words such as “pinion,” meaning wing. Then retell the gulls’ day and return to the text to check it.

excerpt.locator: The Gulls; complete work, 6 source blocks; opens “I”; closes “… huddled on headland and rock— Tis night, for the gulls are asleep.”.

blocks.text: I

Soft is the sky in the mist-kirtled east,
Light is abroad on the sea,
All of the heaven with silver is fleeced,
Holding the sunrise in fee.
Lo! with a flash and uplifting of wings
Down where the long ripples break,
Cometh a bevy of glad-hearted things,
'Tis morn, for the gulls are awake.
II

Slumberous calm on the ocean and shore
Comes with the turn of the tide;
Never a strong-sweeping pinion may soar,
Where the tame fishing-boats ride!
Far and beyond in blue deserts of sea,
Where the wild winds are at play,
There may the spirits of sea-birds be free—
'Tis noon, for the gulls are away.
III

Over the rim of the sunset is blown
Sea-dusk of purple and gold,
Speed now the wanderers back to their own,
Wings the most tireless must fold.
Homeward together at twilight they flock,
Sated with joys of the deep,
Drowsily huddled on headland and rock—
Tis night, for the gulls are asleep.

questions.prompt: How does the first part connect the gulls with morning?
facilitatorNotes: Their sudden wing movement accompanies light and sunrise; the refrain explicitly announces morning because they are awake.
evidence: 'Tis morn, for the gulls are awake.

questions.prompt: Why are the gulls absent from the quiet harbor at noon?
facilitatorNotes: The poem places their freedom farther out where wild winds play, away from tame fishing boats.
evidence: Where the wild winds are at play,

questions.prompt: What does the final part say about even very strong wings?
facilitatorNotes: They still need to fold and rest; the returning flock completes the day’s movement.
evidence: Wings the most tireless must fold.

days.title: How a Fern Bud Unfolds — the opening spiral (excerpt)
days.challenge: Hold several nested plant parts in mind while following their order of opening.
days.focus: A detailed process made vivid through a baby comparison.
days.context: A frond is a fern leaf; pinnæ and pinnules are its smaller divisions. Reread with a simple sketch of nested coils.
days.contentNote: The phrase about a divine origin expresses Comstock’s own belief; the baby and blanket comparisons are her metaphors.
