questions.prompt: Why does a closed fern remind Comstock of a baby?
facilitatorNotes: Its tightly curled divisions resemble closed eyes and fists, and its scales seem like blankets.
evidence: its fists are tightly closed.

questions.prompt: What opens first, and what begins before that opening is finished?
facilitatorNotes: The main stem loosens first; then the pinnæ begin opening before the main coil is completely released.
evidence: First the main stem, or rachis, loosens its coil;

questions.prompt: Why would one quick glance miss much of this process?
facilitatorNotes: The bud contains many nested spirals and can take several days to lose every sign of coiling.
evidence: it may be several days before all signs of the complex coiling disappear.

days.title: Sunrise Along Shore
days.challenge: Notice different groups waking at different times.
days.focus: A working boat within a bright awakening landscape.
days.context: Reread the final two stanzas after picturing the colored water in the first two.

excerpt.locator: Sunrise Along Shore; complete work, 4 source blocks; opens “Athwart the harbor lingers yet The ashen gleam of breaking day, And …”; closes “… at home who sleep And be the first to greet the sun.”.

blocks.text:
Athwart the harbor lingers yet
The ashen gleam of breaking day,
And where the guardian cliffs are set
The noiseless shadows steal away;
But all the winnowed eastern sky
Is flushed with many a tender hue,
And spears of light are smiting through
The ranks where huddled sea-mists fly.

Across the ocean, wan and gray,
Gay fleets of golden ripples come,
For at the birth-hour of the day
The roistering, wayward winds are dumb.
The rocks that stretch to meet the tide
Are smitten with a ruddy glow,
And faint reflections come and go
Where fishing boats at anchor ride.

All life leaps out to greet the light—
The shining sea-gulls dive and soar,
The swallows whirl in dizzy flight,
And sandpeeps flit along the shore.
From every purple landward hill
The banners of the morning fly,
But on the headlands, dim and high,
The fishing hamlets slumber still.

One boat alone beyond the bar
Is sailing outward blithe and free,
To carry sturdy hearts afar
Across those wastes of sparkling sea;
Staunchly to seek what may be won
From out the treasures of the deep,
To toil for those at home who sleep
And be the first to greet the sun.

questions.prompt: What images make sunrise seem to drive darkness away?
facilitatorNotes: Spears of light and fleeing ranks of mist make a peaceful dawn sound like an advancing army.
evidence: spears of light are smiting through

questions.prompt: Is every living thing awake at once?
facilitatorNotes: No; gulls, swallows, and sandpeeps move while the fishing hamlets still sleep.
evidence: The fishing hamlets slumber still.

questions.prompt: What purpose does the one departing boat have beyond enjoying the view?
facilitatorNotes: Its crew goes to work for those asleep at home; beauty and labor occupy the same scene.
evidence: To toil for those at home who sleep

days.title: The Sugar Maple — room to grow (excerpt)
days.challenge: Compare the same tree in open space and in a forest.
days.focus: Description connecting growth, shade, and wind.
days.context: A bole is a trunk, a petiole is a leaf stalk, and leeward means the side sheltered from the wind.

excerpt.locator: The Sugar Maple — room to grow (excerpt); contiguous excerpt, 1 source blocks; opens “THE sugar maple, combining beauty with many kinds of utility, is dear …”; closes “… prevailing winds, and thus makes a one-sided record of their general direction.”.

questions.prompt: How does the tree’s shape differ with its setting?
facilitatorNotes: In open space it has a short trunk and oval head; in a forest its tall trunk rises toward the canopy.
evidence: when planted where it has plenty of room

questions.prompt: Which detail explains why little grass grows under it?
facilitatorNotes: Its dense foliage creates heavy shade, limiting the plants beneath.
evidence: even grass growing but sparsely there.

questions.prompt: How can a tree become a record of prevailing winds?
facilitatorNotes: The author says it grows more on the sheltered side, leaving an uneven shape that indicates the usual wind direction.
evidence: a one-sided record of their general direction.

days.title: Harbor Dawn
days.challenge: Distinguish the speaker’s hopeful prediction from observed sights.
days.focus: Departure surrounded by images of promise.
days.context: A ship leaves in the first red light. “Raiment” means clothing; the hills are imagined wearing mist.

excerpt.locator: Harbor Dawn; complete work, 3 source blocks; opens “There's a hush and stillness calm and deep, For the waves have …”; closes “… ship shall win That crosses the bar when the dawn comes in.”.

blocks.text:
There's a hush and stillness calm and deep,
For the waves have wooed all the winds to sleep
In the shadow of headlands bold and steep;
But some gracious spirit has taken the cup
Of the crystal sky and filled it up
With rosy wine, and in it afar
Has dissolved the pearl of the morning star.

The girdling hills with the night-mist cold
In purple raiment are hooded and stoled
And smit on the brows with fire and gold;
And in the distance the wide, white sea
Is a thing of glamor and wizardry,
With its wild heart lulled to a passing rest,
And the sunrise cradled upon its breast.

With the first red sunlight on mast and spar
A ship is sailing beyond the bar,
Bound to a land that is fair and far;
And those who wait and those who go
Are brave and hopeful, for well they know
Fortune and favor the ship shall win
That crosses the bar when the dawn comes in.

questions.prompt: Why is the beginning unusually quiet?
facilitatorNotes: The waves are imagined as having soothed the winds to sleep, creating calm.
evidence: For the waves have wooed all the winds to sleep

questions.prompt: What comparison joins sunrise and the sea?
facilitatorNotes: The sea cradles the sunrise on its breast, turning the water into a caring figure.
evidence: the sunrise cradled upon its breast.

questions.prompt: Does the poem give proof that the ship will succeed?
facilitatorNotes: No; the ending expresses confidence and hope. Its certainty belongs to the poem’s mood, not a demonstrated future result.
evidence: Fortune and favor the ship shall win

days.title: Mopsa the Fairy — excerpt: a nest unlike any other
days.challenge: Hold several observations together before deciding what lives in the nest.
days.focus: How ordinary details gradually turn a picnic into fantasy.
days.context: Jack is eating cake outdoors with his nurse and baby sister when a sound draws him toward an old tree. Adult and child can alternate paragraphs, with the adult modelling the long descriptions.
days.contentNote: Jack is briefly trapped in the tree and falls with the fairy; the narrator says neither is hurt.

excerpt.locator: CHAPTER I. ABOVE THE CLOUDS.; contiguous excerpt, 9 source blocks; opens “A boy, whom I knew very well, was once going through a …”; closes “… put it into the nest, climbing up to see them eat it.”.

questions.prompt: Which two observations make Jack doubt that the nest contains birds?
facilitatorNotes: He notices the lack of beaks and feathers; ask the child to distinguish observation from his later conclusion that they are fairies.
evidence: Those heads had no beaks

questions.prompt: How does the tree change the situation after Jack climbs inside?
facilitatorNotes: The entrance vanishes, turning exploration into being trapped; the tiny sunbeam is not an ordinary doorway.
evidence: there was no hole at all

questions.prompt: What makes Jack’s decision to share his cake more generous than it first appears?
facilitatorNotes: It is his only food and he may be stuck a long time. Accept the fairies’ small mouths as part of his practical reasoning rather than requiring pure selflessness.
evidence: I have nothing to eat but this cake

days.title: Mopsa the Fairy — excerpt: growing older in minutes
days.challenge: Follow rapid changes in time and appearance while tracking who gives instructions.
days.focus: Comic reversal: the tiny fairies quickly become the experts.
days.context: The trapped Jack has shared his cake with the tiny fairies. A storm arrives, and the fairies take shelter in his pockets.

excerpt.locator: CHAPTER I. ABOVE THE CLOUDS.; contiguous excerpt, 19 source blocks; opens “These young fairies were a long time dividing and munching the cake, …”; closes “… with Jack on her back and all the fairies in his pockets.”.

questions.prompt: How do the fairies’ clothes help Jack notice that they are growing unusually fast?
facilitatorNotes: The pinafore becomes an apron and the boy fairy has a mustache and sword. These details replace an ordinary calendar.
evidence: That is because I am much older now

questions.prompt: Why is Jack’s comparison with a long-division sum funny?
facilitatorNotes: A school task feels preferable to the frightening, unexplained whistle. The comparison gives a familiar measure of his reluctance; children may find the contrast funny in different ways.
evidence: rather have done a long-division sum

questions.prompt: What does the ending reveal about the thing holding Jack’s legs?
facilitatorNotes: It is a large feathered bird carrying him out, not the pony he first imagines. Point to the changing clues.
evidence: It was a large bird

days.title: Mopsa the Fairy — excerpt: Jenny’s warning and the sunrise
days.challenge: Track a helpful instruction while rich visual details compete for attention.
days.focus: The contrast between what Jack needs to remember and what he wants to watch.
days.context: A large bird has lifted Jack and the sleeping fairies out of the tree. They are flying toward Fairyland.

excerpt.locator: CHAPTER I. ABOVE THE CLOUDS.; contiguous excerpt, 25 source blocks; opens “It was so dark that he could see nothing, and he twined …”; closes “… fact, Jack had been out all night, and now it was morning.”.

questions.prompt: What must Jack do if he wants the albatross to take him home?
facilitatorNotes: He must call Jenny; she says she cannot come unless called. Her red and green lights can help him recognise her at night.
evidence: I cannot come unless you do call me

questions.prompt: Which detail makes you doubt that Jack has really stored the warning in his memory?
facilitatorNotes: He says very well but is distracted. This supports concern, not certainty about what he will do later.
evidence: he was not attending

questions.prompt: How does the sunrise change Jack’s explanation of the shapes below?
facilitatorNotes: He first thinks they are mountains and lakes, then recognises clouds as they brighten and break apart. Ask the child to trace the revision.
evidence: I thought they were mountains

days.title: Mopsa the Fairy — excerpt: choosing a boat
days.challenge: Compare a character’s first wish with the practical reasons for a different choice.
days.focus: Why a modest boat fits the journey better than a grand ship.
days.context: At sunrise Jenny carries Jack down toward an enchanted bay. The sleeping fairies must travel onward by river.
days.contentNote: The fantasy mentions sailors thrown into water and names Roman ships and the Spanish Armada. These invented events are not historical evidence; no injuries are described in this excerpt.

excerpt.locator: CHAPTER II. CAPTAIN JACK.; contiguous excerpt, 20 source blocks; opens “All this time the albatross kept dropping down and down like a …”; closes “… he forgot that, because the little boat began to swim so fast.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Jenny reject a large boat for their river journey?
facilitatorNotes: The river is shallow in places. Its physical conditions matter more than how impressive a vessel looks.
evidence: the river in some places is very shallow

questions.prompt: Why does Jack accept Jenny’s choice even though he wants a three-master?
facilitatorNotes: He realises he knows nothing about rigging and sails and trusts her experience. Other explanations must use this admission.
evidence: he did not know anything about sails and rigging

questions.prompt: What is unusual about Jenny’s advice for dealing with hunger?
facilitatorNotes: Jack is told to sleep and eat in a dream, with the real possibility of feeling too full. This is a fantasy rule rather than real nutritional advice.
evidence: Mind you don’t eat too much in your dream

days.title: Mopsa the Fairy — excerpt: the boat learns to slow down
days.challenge: Distinguish a narrator’s explanation, Jack’s commands and his mistaken first impressions.
days.focus: A magical journey still requires care for smaller creatures.
days.context: Jenny has left Jack in a small magical boat with the sleeping fairies. She has told him how to eat in a dream.

excerpt.locator: CHAPTER II. CAPTAIN JACK.; contiguous excerpt, 11 source blocks; opens “She was not sailing, for she had no sail, and he was …”; closes “… between such steep rocks that no one could possibly have climbed them.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator call the boat’s motion swimming?
facilitatorNotes: It has neither a sail nor oars, so familiar explanations fail. The narrator openly searches for the best word.
evidence: I am obliged to call her motion swimming

questions.prompt: What makes Jack tell his boat to travel more gently?
facilitatorNotes: The boat has overturned small nautiluses, and the sea-captain protests. Jack takes responsibility by ordering a slower pace.
evidence: Go at a more gentle pace

questions.prompt: How are the apparent soldiers different from ordinary guards?
facilitatorNotes: They are flamingoes described as regiments. Their still arrangement produces the first misleading impression.
evidence: the guards were not real soldiers, but rose-colored flamingoes

days.title: Mopsa the Fairy — excerpt: the horse answers back
days.challenge: Notice clues whose meanings Jack does not yet understand, including “works” and “wind up.”
days.focus: Dialogue makes the unfamiliar country both puzzling and comic.
days.context: Jack’s boat has reached a quiet bay beside the wonderful river. He hopes to discover whether he has arrived in Fairyland.

excerpt.locator: CHAPTER III. WINDING-UP TIME.; contiguous excerpt, 31 source blocks; opens “Jack looked at these hot, brown rocks, first on the left bank …”; closes “… out some day, perhaps,” he continued, “whether horses can talk or not.””.

questions.prompt: How does the boat respond when Jack wishes to land?
facilitatorNotes: It immediately changes course, as though it understands him. His spoken wish has consequences before he plans them.
evidence: the boat altered her course

questions.prompt: Why is the horse’s complaint about “gee” and “wo” reasonable?
facilitatorNotes: The women give conflicting instructions to go and stop. Even a willing horse cannot follow both at once.
evidence: what’s a fellow to do when you say them both together?

questions.prompt: How does the horse challenge Jack’s belief about horses in his own world?
facilitatorNotes: Jack says they cannot talk; the horse says they will not. This makes an assumed inability into a possible choice.
evidence: You mean they won’t

days.title: Mopsa the Fairy — excerpt: a country that heals horses
days.challenge: Separate the fantasy’s invented rules from its serious concern for mistreated animals.
days.focus: Reversed ageing imagines a way to repair past harm.
days.context: Jack is walking beside two washer-women and their talking horse, Boney. The women have hinted that their own bodies have clockwork parts. The adult leads the reading of this longer scene; invite the child to reread a chosen short exchange.
days.contentNote: The passage refers to beating horses, exhausted animals and their deaths. Ingelow wrote in 1869, when the treatment of racehorses and working horses was a public concern in Britain; the healing country is her invention.

excerpt.locator: CHAPTER III. WINDING-UP TIME.; contiguous excerpt, 35 source blocks; opens ““Shall I?” said Jack, very earnestly.”; closes “… her chain. She’s not like the goods they turn out in Clerkenwell.””.

questions.prompt: What future do the women promise Boney, and how does he react?
facilitatorNotes: They promise youth, freedom and happy meadows; he perks up and moves faster. His response links hope to visible action.
evidence: pricked up his ears and quickened his pace

questions.prompt: Why is this country especially suited to horses that have suffered?
facilitatorNotes: They arrive old and hurt, receive care, and gradually become young again. Describe it as a fictional repair of suffering, not a scientific or religious fact.
evidence: bring them up to be young and happy again

questions.prompt: Which final clues show that Faxa is unlike an ordinary person?
facilitatorNotes: Jack hears ticking; the horse calls her machine-made and mentions her chain. The regular steps now have a new explanation.
evidence: She’s machine-made

days.title: Mopsa the Fairy — excerpt: Lady Betty and winding-up time
days.challenge: Connect a horse’s history with the rules of the border country, then use clockwork clues to understand Jack’s danger.
days.focus: A custom that helps the residents becomes frightening to a visitor.
days.context: Jack has run after the groom and Dow to find Lady Betty, whom he expects to be a lady. Later in the scene he asks about the country and follows a ringing bell.
days.contentNote: The groom tells how Lady Betty was spurred and beaten at a jump, broke both forelegs and was shot. Later a groom suggests making a keyhole in Jack’s head; Jack escapes.

excerpt.locator: CHAPTER III. WINDING-UP TIME.; contiguous excerpt, 30 source blocks; opens “Jack was more and more startled, and so glad to get his …”; closes “… the boat, and fell into a doze, and then into a dream.”.

questions.prompt: What does the groom say this country is for, and how does Lady Betty’s story show it?
facilitatorNotes: It is a border country where harm done in the human world is set right; Lady Betty was driven beyond her powers and killed, and is being made “all right again”. Discuss why a boy who reminds her of a jockey upsets her.
evidence: where things are set right again that people have caused to go wrong in the world
Then they shot her.

questions.prompt: What finally explains the earlier talk about weights, works and ticking?
facilitatorNotes: The inhabitants must be wound like watches; the Queen uses keys in their heads. This completes the pattern of clockwork clues.
evidence: Winding us up, to be sure

questions.prompt: Why does Jack refuse to take his turn even though the groom insists?
facilitatorNotes: He has no keyhole and does not need winding; the suggestion of making one frightens him. His different needs justify refusing conformity.
evidence: There’s no key-hole in my head

questions.prompt: What gives Jack a chance to escape, and what does he check afterward?
facilitatorNotes: The residents initially cannot run because they need winding; his boat carries him away and he checks the fairies. Connect his escape with the world’s rule.
evidence: they could not run after him, because they wanted winding up

days.title: Mopsa the Fairy — excerpt: the ravens in the boat
days.challenge: Notice when characters say one thing and mean another, and how one mistake changes Jack’s journey.
days.focus: Flattery hides the ravens’ purpose; the lost fairy is named only through the ones who remain.
days.context: Jack has escaped down the river and fallen asleep in the boat with the four sleeping fairies in his pockets. The new chapter opens with a short poem.
days.contentNote: A raven seizes one of the fairies and eats it; Jack blames himself.

excerpt.locator: CHAPTER IV. BEES AND OTHER FELLOW-CREATURES.; contiguous excerpt, 25 source blocks; opens “The dove laid some little sticks, Then began to coo; The gnat …”; closes “… was a very fierce-looking gentleman; the other two were Roxaletta and Mopsa.”.

questions.prompt: What do the ravens say to each other, and how do they speak to Jack?
facilitatorNotes: They plan to eat the fairies, then call him “my young master” and claim not to be hungry. Ask the child to find one polite phrase that hides the plan.
evidence: fairies are delicate eating indeed
We must speak Jack fair if we want to get at them.

questions.prompt: Why do most of the ravens fly away after Jack laughs?
facilitatorNotes: They think he is mocking them because he has guessed their purpose. His honest laugh about the three moons protects him for a while without his knowing it.
evidence: there is nothing that birds hate so much as to be laughed at

questions.prompt: How does the last raven trick Jack into giving her what she wants?
facilitatorNotes: She warns that water-snakes want the fairies, so he takes one out to check it. Some readers will call Jack careless, others the trick clever; the text has Jack call himself foolish.
evidence: Jack was so thrown off his guard that he snatched one fairy out
to think what a foolish boy he had been

days.title: Mopsa the Fairy — excerpt: a market with mushroom roofs
days.challenge: Build a setting from colour, shape and texture, then follow an unexpected exchange.
days.focus: The market mixes familiar shopping with impossible buildings and payment rules.
days.context: A raven took one of Jack’s four fairies in the night. Morning reveals a busy market beside the water. The adult reads this extended scene aloud at an unhurried pace; the child can follow the action and join the discussion.
days.contentNote: The narrator uses “gypsies”, the period word for Roma people, and describes the imaginary traders by their looks; these are Ingelow’s 1869 labels.

excerpt.locator: CHAPTER IV. BEES AND OTHER FELLOW-CREATURES.; contiguous excerpt, 29 source blocks; opens “Presently, however, Jack forgot to be unhappy, for two of the moons …”; closes “… she made a pretty little courtesy, and went away to her customers.”.

questions.prompt: What makes Jack unsure whether the round shelters are tents or mushrooms?
facilitatorNotes: Their central pillars, rounded canopies and coloured flutings resemble mushrooms but shelter shoppers. Accept either as the impression, keeping his uncertainty.
evidence: impossible to be sure whether these were real tents or gigantic mushrooms

questions.prompt: Why is Jack’s sixpence returned even though it is a good coin?
facilitatorNotes: The bees dislike its being old, dirty-looking and bent. Monetary value does not decide what this seller will accept.
evidence: They like things to be neat and new

questions.prompt: Why is a whistle a useful substitute for money here?
facilitatorNotes: It can call the bees home when flowers have been gathered. The new payment serves the household’s particular needs.
evidence: They love to be called home

days.title: Mopsa the Fairy — excerpt: the parrots want more than food
days.challenge: Follow changing motives in dialogue rather than treating the loudest speaker as fully explained.
days.focus: Objects such as maize and a handkerchief carry different kinds of comfort.
days.context: Jack is at the enchanted market after trading his whistle for food. Caged parrots are trying to attract the shoppers’ attention. The adult leads the reading of this longer scene; invite the child to reread a chosen short exchange.
days.contentNote: The parrots describe captivity and call “gypsies” (the period word for Roma people) their enemies; the hostility is the parrots’, in Ingelow’s 1869 fantasy.

excerpt.locator: CHAPTER IV. BEES AND OTHER FELLOW-CREATURES.; contiguous excerpt, 33 source blocks; opens “There were some very strange creatures also, about the same height as …”; closes “… and he listened to what he had to say the more attentively.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the parrot prefer a handkerchief to the maize already bought for him?
facilitatorNotes: He wants to express sadness and feel noticed, not only be fed. Children may note that food remains necessary; the passage contrasts kinds of need.
evidence: it hurts my feelings

questions.prompt: What sudden change follows Jack’s touching the cage?
facilitatorNotes: The parrot and the others go quiet and recognise him as a boy. The action reveals something that appearance alone did not.
evidence: I had no notion you were a boy till you touched my cage

questions.prompt: What suggests that the borrowed handkerchief may have a purpose beyond wiping tears?
facilitatorNotes: They roll it into a ball, hide it under a wing and call it good luck. This supports a prediction, but the precise use is not yet supplied.
evidence: instead of using it they rolled it up into a ball

days.title: Mopsa the Fairy — excerpt: travelling backward instead of far away
days.challenge: Keep two kinds of knowledge in view: reading letters and understanding an invented world.
days.focus: Mopsa challenges Jack’s assumption that he must always be the teacher.
days.context: Much later, Jack and the growing Mopsa are with an apple-woman in Fairyland. Jack wants to teach Mopsa to read, but she knows things about this world that he does not.
days.contentNote: Ingelow’s account of the world before people is part of her fantasy.

excerpt.locator: CHAPTER X. MOPSA LEARNS HER LETTERS.; contiguous excerpt, 17 source blocks; opens ““How ashamed I am,” Jack said, “to think that you don’t know …”; closes “… while you went through those countries; but these are the real Fairylands.””.

questions.prompt: How does the conversation overturn Jack’s opening judgment about Mopsa’s ignorance?
facilitatorNotes: She cannot read letters, but explains Fairyland’s relation to time while Jack struggles. Different knowledge can belong to different people.
evidence: when I’m a little older, I’ll explain it all to you

questions.prompt: What does Mopsa mean by saying Jenny flew “back” rather than far away?
facilitatorNotes: She describes time travel into a past before humans, not merely a long flight across distance. Keep this an invented explanation.
evidence: not fly with you a long way off, but a long way back

questions.prompt: Why does Jack bring up the old ships, and how does Mopsa answer?
facilitatorNotes: Ships made by humans seem to contradict a time before humans. Mopsa separates the border countries from real Fairylands; discuss whether that satisfies the reader.
evidence: That was a border country

days.title: Mopsa the Fairy — excerpt: two Jacks find the hidden door
days.challenge: Recognise a story told after its outcome, and follow how pride gives way to cooperation.
days.focus: The adventure’s turning point is a new way of seeing what seemed frightening.
days.context: Near the end, Mopsa has become a queen. Jack and a fairy boy who looks like him have just freed enchanted people. At a feast, they recount how they did it.
days.contentNote: The scene includes eerie moaning and enchanted captives, but no graphic injury. Explain that Jack and his fairy double are different characters.

excerpt.locator: CHAPTER XVI. FAILURE.; contiguous excerpt, 14 source blocks; opens “Mopsa was not happy, Jack was sure of that, for she often …”; closes “… It fitted, and out they all came, as you have been told.”.

questions.prompt: How does Jack turn the boy-king’s demand to go first into a different view of honour?
facilitatorNotes: He calls going first helpful scouting and says his own Queen goes last. The competing definitions expose how arbitrary the quarrel can be.
evidence: you’ve gone in first to find the way for me

questions.prompt: What ends the quarrel without either boy winning the argument?
facilitatorNotes: A frightening sound makes them take hands and face a shared problem. Fear has changed their priorities.
evidence: instantly made them friends

questions.prompt: Why is recognising the “sticks” as antlers important?
facilitatorNotes: It turns an unclear, frightening scene into a herd of stags; the herd then moves and leads them onward. Naming accurately changes action.
evidence: No; they are antlers!

days.title: Mopsa the Fairy — excerpt: Mopsa’s farewell
days.challenge: Distinguish Jack’s fearful interpretation from what another character’s actions suggest.
days.focus: A farewell can contain love and grief even when friends must separate.
days.context: The feast is ending, but Mopsa is sad. A white fairy reminds Jack of Jenny, the bird who promised to carry him home. A fairy boy resembling Jack will remain with Mopsa.
days.contentNote: This scene centres on a painful separation and a child’s fear of being replaced.

excerpt.locator: CHAPTER XVI. FAILURE.; contiguous excerpt, 19 source blocks; opens “Now all this time Mopsa sat between the two Jacks, and she …”; closes “How beautiful it looked in the evening sunshine, and how Jack cried!”.

questions.prompt: Why does hearing Jenny’s name make Jack sorrowful rather than relieved?
facilitatorNotes: It reminds him that he can and is expected to leave. The solution to getting home now threatens his wish to stay with Mopsa.
evidence: he longed to stay

questions.prompt: Jack thinks Mopsa does not need him. What details make that judgment less certain?
facilitatorNotes: She is mournful, sighs and cries when she kisses him. These details allow grief and attachment even though she cannot keep him there.
evidence: her tears fell on his cheek

questions.prompt: How do the closing doors and the silence change the feeling of the castle?
facilitatorNotes: Its earlier music and welcome are replaced by separation and stillness. Ask for emotional language supported by those changes, not one required adjective.
evidence: no more fairy music sounded

days.title: Mopsa the Fairy — excerpt: Jenny carries Jack home
days.challenge: Trace a changing emotion across magical distance and familiar domestic details.
days.focus: Returning home does not erase sadness at once, but it changes the scale of the adventure.
days.context: Mopsa has said farewell and the castle doors have closed. Jack must decide what to do as the fairy world changes around him. The excerpt ends just as his mother begins another poem. The adult leads the reading of this longer scene; invite the child to reread a chosen short exchange.
days.contentNote: The passage carries forward sadness over leaving a friend. Fairy time is an invented rule rather than a real explanation of time zones.

excerpt.locator: CHAPTER XVI. FAILURE.; contiguous excerpt, 21 source blocks; opens “Suddenly he perceived that reeds were growing up between him and the …”; closes “… again to read, and this time it was about the Shepherd Lady:—”.

questions.prompt: How do the reeds make Jack’s separation from the castle physical as well as emotional?
facilitatorNotes: They rise around him and block the view despite his moving backward. The setting prevents a simple return.
evidence: the last glimpse of the fairy castle was hidden

questions.prompt: Which details show that Jenny’s earlier promise has been kept?
facilitatorNotes: Jack calls her, sees the red and green lights, and she arrives to carry him. Her remembered name enables the return.
evidence: Here I am.

questions.prompt: How does sitting on his father’s knee change Jack’s view of his journey?
facilitatorNotes: He compares his own safe place with the fairies in his pocket, feels the familiar adults’ size and comfort, and is glad to be home. Accept lingering sadness alongside comfort.
evidence: on the whole, he was glad he had come back

days.title: The Divine Image
days.challenge: Follow abstract qualities as they become human features.
days.focus: A religious argument for care across differences.
days.context: Read this poem with an adult. Its historical group labels need explanation, while its ending asks readers to recognize humanity across religious difference.
days.contentNote: This poem expresses the author’s Christian belief. Discuss that viewpoint without asking readers to share it. “Heathen” was a dismissive label for people outside certain religions; “Turk” is used here as a historical religious shorthand. These are the author’s dated categories, not labels the reader should apply.

evidence: To Mercy, Pity, Peace, and Love,

facilitatorNotes: It gives mercy a heart, pity a face, love a human form, and peace clothing.
evidence: For Mercy has a human heart;

facilitatorNotes: It says all must love the human form even among people named as religious outsiders, locating God where these qualities dwell.
evidence: And all must love the human form,

facilitatorNotes: Its picturesque twisted branches, shade, and suitability for birds make it a place she wants to live.

days.title: An April Night
days.challenge: Use “like” and other clues to separate natural sights from imagined beings.
days.focus: An ordinary night transformed by folklore.
days.context: Dryads are imagined tree spirits, and Will-o’-the-Wisp is a traditional name for a mysterious marsh light. These are poetic figures.

excerpt.locator: An April Night; complete work, 4 source blocks; opens “The moon comes up o'er the deeps of the woods, And the …”; closes “… us in meadow and mere The spell of a hundred vanished Springs.”.

blocks.text:
The moon comes up o'er the deeps of the woods,
And the long, low dingles that hide in the hills,
Where the ancient beeches are moist with buds
Over the pools and the whimpering rills;

And with her the mists, like dryads that creep
From their oaks, or the spirits of pine-hid springs,
Who hold, while the eyes of the world are asleep,
With the wind on the hills their gay revellings.

Down on the marshlands with flicker and glow
Wanders Will-o'-the-Wisp through the night,
Seeking for witch-gold lost long ago
By the glimmer of goblin lantern-light.

The night is a sorceress, dusk-eyed and dear,
Akin to all eerie and elfin things,
Who weaves about us in meadow and mere
The spell of a hundred vanished Springs.

questions.prompt: What small detail places the scene in spring?
facilitatorNotes: Beech buds appear, linking the woods to new growth rather than bare winter.
evidence: the ancient beeches are moist with buds

questions.prompt: How does the speaker make drifting mist seem alive?
facilitatorNotes: It is compared to dryads creeping out of trees and spirits gathering with the wind.
evidence: the mists, like dryads that creep

questions.prompt: What does calling night a sorceress do for the whole scene?
facilitatorNotes: It gathers the earlier magical images into one powerful figure casting an old springtime spell.
evidence: The night is a sorceress, dusk-eyed and dear,

days.title: The Pine — describing great size (excerpt)
days.challenge: Compare measurements while noticing which object the author actually has nearby.
days.focus: Scale made concrete through a cone.
days.context: The passage moves from very tall trees to a cone on the writer’s desk. The numbers are the historical author’s reported measurements.

questions.prompt: How do the reported heights of eastern white pine and western sugar pine compare?
facilitatorNotes: The white pine range is 150–200 feet, and the sugar pine range 200–300 feet, with 200 appearing in both.
evidence: from two to three hundred feet in height;

questions.prompt: Why can a thick trunk still look slender?
facilitatorNotes: The enormous height changes the visual proportion; a 6–10 foot diameter can seem slender against that height.
evidence: yet it looks slender, so tall is the tree.

questions.prompt: Which measurement comes from an object clearly at hand?
facilitatorNotes: The 22-inch cone on her desk, unlike the more general statements about trees.
evidence: A sugar pine cone on my desk measures 22 inches in length

days.title: The Wood Pool
days.challenge: Read modal words carefully to distinguish possibility from assertion.
days.focus: A shaded place inviting imagination.
days.context: Pan, dryads, and wood-nymphs are figures from ancient Greek stories. The poem imagines them in a quiet pool’s setting.

excerpt.locator: The Wood Pool; complete work, 4 source blocks; opens “Here is a voice that soundeth low and far And lyric—voice of …”; closes “… place, Or lover yielding to the immortal dream Of one beloved face.”.

blocks.text:
Here is a voice that soundeth low and far
And lyric—voice of wind among the pines,
Where the untroubled, glimmering waters are,
And sunlight seldom shines.

Elusive shadows linger shyly here,
And wood-flowers blow, like pale, sweet spirit-bloom,
And white, slim birches whisper, mirrored clear
In the pool's lucent gloom.

Here Pan might pipe, or wandering dryad kneel
To view her loveliness beside the brim,
Or laughing wood-nymphs from the byways steal
To dance around its rim.

'Tis such a witching spot as might beseem
A seeker for young friendship's trysting place,
Or lover yielding to the immortal dream
Of one beloved face.

questions.prompt: What makes the pool feel secluded?
facilitatorNotes: Sunlight seldom reaches it, shadows linger, and the wind sounds distant among pines.
evidence: And sunlight seldom shines.

questions.prompt: What do the birches seem to do in the water?
facilitatorNotes: They whisper and appear as clear reflections; sound and sight work together in the image.
evidence: white, slim birches whisper, mirrored clear

questions.prompt: Does the poet claim that Pan was actually seen there?
facilitatorNotes: No; “might” marks an imagined possibility fitting the magical atmosphere.
evidence: Here Pan might pipe, or wandering dryad kneel

days.title: Alice, chapter VII, part 1: An unwelcoming welcome
days.challenge: Take dialogue roles and test the reversed sentences with an everyday example.
days.focus: Rules of politeness and the logic of reversing words.
days.context: Alice has wandered through Wonderland and now reaches a tea table shared by the Hatter, March Hare, and sleepy Dormouse.
days.contentNote: The characters use a sleeping animal as a cushion and speak rudely to one another.

excerpt.locator: CHAPTER VII; contiguous excerpt, 21 source blocks; opens “THERE was a table set out under a tree in front of …”; closes “… over all she could remember about ravens and writing-desks, which wasn't much.”.

questions.prompt: What makes the cry of no room unconvincing?
facilitatorNotes: The table is large and the three hosts are crowded at one corner. Their claim seems intended to exclude Alice rather than describe the available space.
evidence: The table was a large one

questions.prompt: How do Alice and the March Hare disagree about what counts as rude?
facilitatorNotes: Alice objects to an offer of nonexistent wine; the Hare objects to her arriving without an invitation. Each notices the other person’s breach of manners.
evidence: It wasn't very civil of you to sit down without being invited

questions.prompt: Why are seeing everything you eat and eating everything you see different?
facilitatorNotes: The first allows many visible things to remain uneaten; the second would require eating them. Help the child apply the distinction to a cup or chair at the table.
evidence: I eat what I see

days.title: Alice, chapter VII, part 2: A watch and a person called Time
days.challenge: Read the exchange once for the scene and again to locate two different meanings of time.
days.focus: Wordplay that treats an abstract idea as a person.
days.context: Alice’s tea companions turn from riddles to a peculiar watch. Their explanations use ordinary words in unexpected ways.
days.contentNote: The Hatter pours hot tea on the Dormouse’s nose; this is unkind treatment in the story.

excerpt.locator: CHAPTER VII; contiguous excerpt, 27 source blocks; opens “The Hatter was the first to break the silence. "What day of …”; closes “"Is that the way you manage?" Alice asked.”.

questions.prompt: Why does calling the butter best fail to answer the Hatter’s complaint?
facilitatorNotes: Quality butter is still unsuitable for watch machinery. The Hare defends the wrong feature of his attempted repair.
evidence: It was the best butter

questions.prompt: How does the riddle’s ending differ from Alice’s expectation?
facilitatorNotes: Neither questioner knows an answer. She expected a puzzle that could be solved, so she judges it a waste of time.
evidence: I haven't the slightest idea

questions.prompt: What does the Hatter change when he says Time is him?
facilitatorNotes: He personifies time, so beating musical time becomes mistreating someone and a clock can be influenced through friendship.
evidence: It's him.

days.title: Alice, chapter VII, part 3: The endless tea
days.challenge: Sing or speak the short verses, then trace the everyday consequences of time stopping.
days.focus: An impossible rule followed through to practical problems.
days.context: The Hatter explains a quarrel with Time. A familiar tune and an unusual story give Alice more things to question.
days.contentNote: The Queen threatens execution, and the Dormouse is pinched; these are fantasy threats and mistreatment.

excerpt.locator: CHAPTER VII; contiguous excerpt, 37 source blocks; opens “The Hatter shook his head mournfully. "Not I!" he replied. "We quarrelled …”; closes “… "I won't interrupt you again. I dare say there may be one."”.

questions.prompt: How does the Hatter’s song change the familiar star song?
facilitatorNotes: It replaces the star with a bat and compares it to a tea-tray. Familiar rhythm makes the absurd substitutions more noticeable.
evidence: Like a tea-tray in the sky.

questions.prompt: Why do they need so many cups if it is always tea-time?
facilitatorNotes: They cannot reach a time between teas to wash cups, so they move to unused settings. Alice’s question about completing the circle exposes an unresolved problem.
evidence: we've no time to wash the things between whiles.

questions.prompt: How does the Dormouse respond when Alice says a treacle diet would make the sisters ill?
facilitatorNotes: He agrees they were ill instead of correcting the improbable story. Her objection becomes another detail within its logic.
evidence: So they were

days.title: Alice, chapter VII, part 4: Drawing muchness
days.challenge: Let the child read the dialogue independently where comfortable, then discuss how draw changes meaning.
days.focus: The point at which curiosity gives way to leaving an unpleasant situation.
days.context: The Dormouse’s story continues, while the tea guests shift places and Alice tries to understand what its words mean.
days.contentNote: The guests pinch the Dormouse and try to put it into a teapot. These comic actions are unkind.

excerpt.locator: CHAPTER VII; contiguous excerpt, 21 source blocks; opens “"One, indeed!" said the Dormouse indignantly. However, he consented to go on. …”; closes “… in the beautiful garden, among the bright flower-beds and the cool fountains.”.

questions.prompt: Who actually benefits when everyone moves to a new place?
facilitatorNotes: Only the Hatter improves his situation; Alice inherits spilled milk. The apparently shared solution serves its proposer best.
evidence: The Hatter was the only one who got any advantage

facilitatorNotes: It can mean pulling liquid from a well or making a picture. A drawing of memory or muchness adds the difficulty of picturing an abstract idea.

questions.prompt: What shows that Alice has learned from her earlier difficulties in the hall?
facilitatorNotes: She gets the key and unlocks the garden door before shrinking. Her ordered actions show deliberate problem-solving after the disordered conversation.
evidence: began by taking the little golden key

days.title: Alice, chapter VIII, part 1: Painted roses
days.challenge: Connect the playing-card descriptions with what the characters can and cannot see. For this longer scene, the adult reads the source aloud and the child rereads only a chosen short quotation.
days.focus: Courage and concealment under an unreasonable ruler.
days.context: Alice finally enters the garden she has wanted to reach. Its gardeners have an urgent reason for changing the roses’ color.
days.contentNote: The Queen repeatedly orders beheadings; Alice protects the gardeners, and no execution occurs in this scene.

excerpt.locator: CHAPTER VIII; contiguous excerpt, 33 source blocks; opens “A LARGE rose-tree stood near the entrance of the garden: the roses …”; closes “… and Alice joined the procession, wondering very much what would happen next.”.

questions.prompt: Why are the gardeners painting white roses red?
facilitatorNotes: They planted the wrong tree and fear punishment. The disguise attempts to hide a mistake instead of repairing it.
evidence: we put a white one in by mistake

questions.prompt: Why can the Queen not identify the three gardeners on the ground?
facilitatorNotes: They are face down, and their card backs are identical. The fantasy’s playing-card bodies create a practical difficulty.
evidence: the pattern on their backs was the same

questions.prompt: How does Alice turn her refusal to allow a beheading into action?
facilitatorNotes: She hides the gardeners in a flower-pot; the soldiers fail to find them. Her response has an immediate protective result.
evidence: she put them into a large flower-pot

days.title: Alice, chapter VIII, part 2: Living croquet
days.challenge: Build a mental picture of one turn; pause through the long description of moving equipment.
days.focus: Why a game needs shared rules as well as equipment.
days.context: Alice joins the Queen’s game, but the equipment and rules refuse to behave as she expects.
days.contentNote: The game uses live animals, and the Queen threatens players with execution. These are absurd, unkind fantasy actions.

days.title: Alice, chapter VIII, part 3: A head without a body

days.title: Alice, chapter IX, part 2: Orders and pardons
days.challenge: Compare what the Queen says, what the King does, and what the Gryphon reports.
days.focus: Testing frightening statements against what actually happens.
days.context: The Queen interrupts Alice and the Duchess. After more croquet, Alice meets a Gryphon and a sorrowful Mock Turtle.
days.contentNote: The Queen threatens executions; the King pardons everyone and the Gryphon says the threats are not carried out.

evidence: if he doesn't begin

days.challenge: Say the school words aloud with adult help, then explain one joke independently.
days.focus: Sound-alike words produce a whole imaginary curriculum.
days.context: The Mock Turtle remembers school under the sea. His memories resemble Alice’s schooling but twist familiar names and expectations.
days.contentNote: Carroll is parodying the lessons and rote learning of Victorian schoolrooms.

facilitatorNotes: Taught us sounds like tortoise in the joke. The explanation depends on sound rather than the teacher’s actual species.

facilitatorNotes: Living underwater makes washing seem unnecessary; a household service is also being treated as a school subject. Explain extras as separately charged services.

facilitatorNotes: Hours decrease until a holiday, but continuing the rule becomes troublesome beyond zero. Her question tests whether the pun-based system can keep working.

days.title: Alice, chapter X, part 1: An invitation to dance
days.challenge: Read the song aloud twice, joining in the refrain and identifying which speaker wants what.
days.focus: A repeated invitation meets a repeated refusal.
days.context: The Mock Turtle and Gryphon explain the Lobster Quadrille and perform its first figure and song.
days.contentNote: The imaginary dance throws lobsters into the sea; the performers tread on Alice’s toes.

facilitatorNotes: Their enthusiasm makes them jump, shout, and caper; then they suddenly sit sadly again. The shift contrasts energetic memory with their usual sorrow.

facilitatorNotes: The whiting says moving away from one shore brings them nearer another. This reframes the same journey without answering every danger the snail may fear.

days.title: Alice, chapter X, part 2: A porpoise or a purpose

days.contentNote: Alice nearly mentions eating the creatures she is discussing; this is a source of social awkwardness in the fantasy.

evidence: Soles and eels, of course

days.focus: Uncertain performance, comic poems, and a sudden interruption.
days.context: Alice begins to tell her adventures, but her listeners turn the visit into another recitation lesson. Her familiar words become strange poems.
days.contentNote: The poem hints that a Panther may eat an Owl, but the line is interrupted. The creatures pressure Alice to perform.

facilitatorNotes: It boasts when sharks are absent but becomes timid when they return with the water. The contrast exposes boastfulness without safety.

facilitatorNotes: The Panther takes all the food while the Owl receives the dish and spoon. The polite wording makes the unequal division more pointed.
evidence: While the Owl had the dish as its share of the treat.

facilitatorNotes: Alice hurries toward the trial while his mournful song fades behind her. Sound creates a lingering connection even as the action changes.

days.title: Alice, chapter XI, part 1: A trial begins

days.contentNote: The King threatens a nervous witness with execution. Alice takes a juror’s pencil without permission.

excerpt.locator: CHAPTER XI; contiguous excerpt, 28 source blocks; opens “THE King and Queen of Hearts were seated on their throne when …”; closes “… bit a large piece out of his teacup instead of the bread-and-butter.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the jurors’ busy writing fail to impress Alice?
facilitatorNotes: Before hearing evidence they write their names, then copy her insult. Activity is being mistaken for useful record keeping.

questions.prompt: Why does the Rabbit stop the King’s first request for a verdict?
facilitatorNotes: No witnesses have yet been heard. The trial needs evidence before a decision about guilt.
evidence: There's a great deal to come before that!

facilitatorNotes: Not owning it does not prove theft: he keeps hats to sell. The King leaps to a conclusion without allowing the explanation.

days.title: Alice, chapter XI, part 2: The frightened witness
days.challenge: Track the difference between a speaker’s intended meaning and the King’s interpretation.
days.focus: Threats and literal meanings disrupt testimony.
days.context: Alice begins growing again while the Hatter struggles to give evidence. The court’s demands increase his confusion.
days.contentNote: Threats of execution recur. Guinea-pigs are put into bags and sat upon; this is cruel fantasy treatment.

excerpt.locator: CHAPTER XI; contiguous excerpt, 34 source blocks; opens “Just at this moment Alice felt a very curious sensation, which puzzled …”; closes “… was out of sight before the officer could get to the door.”.

questions.prompt: How does the Dormouse distinguish his own growth from Alice’s?

days.title: Alice, chapter XI, part 3: The next witness

days.focus: An inquiry that repeatedly loses sight of its purpose.
days.context: The cook arrives carrying pepper. The court tries to question her, but confusion soon shifts attention elsewhere.
days.contentNote: The Queen threatens and orders mistreatment of the Dormouse; the cook leaves during the commotion.

questions.prompt: How does Alice recognize the cook before seeing her clearly?
facilitatorNotes: People near the door sneeze because of the pepper-box. Their reaction supplies a clue before an introduction.
evidence: began sneezing all at once

facilitatorNotes: It asks about a recipe, not the accused person’s actions. The absurd answers and Dormouse interruption carry the court farther from the charge.
evidence: What are tarts made of?

questions.prompt: What does Alice’s assessment of the evidence suggest about her attention?
facilitatorNotes: She notices the court has learned very little despite all the questioning. Her next surprise is that she herself will be called.
evidence: they haven't got much evidence yet

days.title: Alice, chapter XII, part 1: Rule Forty-two
days.challenge: Distinguish accidental harm, truthful testimony, and an invented rule; read Alice’s objections with growing confidence.
days.focus: A witness begins to question the authority directing the trial.
days.context: Alice is called to testify and forgets how large she has become. She helps repair an accident, then challenges the King’s attempt to remove her.
days.contentNote: The jury tumbles out of its box; the scene treats the fall comically without serious injury.

excerpt.locator: CHAPTER XII; contiguous excerpt, 21 source blocks; opens “"HERE!" cried Alice, quite forgetting in the flurry of the moment how …”; closes “… your verdict," he said to the jury, in a low trembling voice.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the fallen jury remind Alice of goldfish?
facilitatorNotes: She once upset a bowl of fish and urgently collected them. That memory shapes her rescue response even though jurors do not need water.

blocks.text:
Comrades, up! Let us row down stream in this first rare dawnlight,
While far in the clear north-west the late moon whitens and wanes;
Before us the sun will rise, deep-purpling headland and islet,
It is well to meet him thus, with the life astir in our veins!

The wakening birds will sing for us in the woods wind-shaken,
And the solitude of the hills will be broken by hymns to the light,
As we sweep past drowsing hamlets, still feathered by dreams of slumber,
And leave behind us the shadows that fell with the falling of night.

The young day's strength is ours in sinew and thew and muscle,
We are filled and thrilled with the spirit that dwells in the waste and wold,
Glamor of wind and water, charm of the wildernesses—
Oh, the dear joy of it, greater than human hearts can hold!

While the world's tired children sleep we bend to our oars with faces
Set in our eager gladness towards the morning's gate;
Lo, 'tis the sweet of the day! On, comrades mine, for beyond us
All its dower of beauty, its glory and wonder, wait.

Here on a hill of the occident stand we shoulder to shoulder,
Comrades tried and true through a mighty swath of the years!
Spring harps glad laughter through us, and ministrant rains of the autumn
Sing us again the songs of ancient dolor and tears.

The glory of sunrise smites on our fair, free brows uplifted
When the silver-kirtled day steps over the twilight's bars;
At evening we look adown into valleys hearted with sunset,
And we whisper old lore together under the smouldering stars.

Crescent moons of the summer gleam through our swaying branches,
Knee-deep in fern we stand while the days of the sun-time go;
And the winds of winter love us—the keen, gay winds of the winter,
Coming to our gray arms from over the plains of snow.

Down in the valleys beneath us is wooing and winning and wedding,
Down in the long, dim valleys earth-children wail and weep;
But here on these free hills we grow and are strong and flourish,
Comrades shoulder to shoulder our watch of the years to keep.

excerpt.inlineReason: The night prints the mirror-printed title as .YKCOWREBBAJ with a full stop (U+002E); the Kellscraft transcription has a middle dot there (·YKCOWREBBAJ, U+00B7 from ·); the edition’s correction note does not name this reading and its ledger is not in the repository, so the library keeps the transcription’s reading until the scan is checked.

blocks.text: The King was saying, "I assure you, my dear, I turned cold to the very ends of my whiskers!"
To which the Queen replied, "You haven't got any whiskers."
"The horror of that moment," the King went on, "I shall never, never forget!"
"You will, though," the Queen said, "if you don't make a memorandum of it."

Alice looked on with great interest as the King took an enormous memorandum-book out of his pocket, and began writing. A sudden thought struck her, and she took hold of the end of the pencil, which came some way over his shoulder, and began writing for him.

The poor King looked puzzled and unhappy, and struggled with the pencil for some time without saying anything; but Alice was too strong for him, and at last he panted out, "My dear! I really must get a thinner pencil. I can't manage this one a bit; it writes all manner of things that I don't intend --"

"What manner of things?" said the Queen, looking over the book (in which Alice had put "The White Knight is sliding down the poker. He balances very badly"). "That's not a memorandum of your feelings!"

There was a book lying near Alice on the table, and while she sat watching the White King (for she was still a little anxious about him, and had the ink all ready to throw over him, in case he fainted again), she turned over the leaves, to find some part that she could read, "for it's all in some language I don't know," she said to herself.
It was like this:
.YKCOWREBBAJ

sevot yhtils eht dna ,gillirb sawT'
:ebaw eht ni elbmig dna eryg diD
,sevogorob eht erew ysmim llA
.ebargtuo shtar emom eht dnA
She puzzled over this for some time, but at last a bright thought struck her. "Why, it's a looking-glass-book, of course! And if I hold it up to a glass, the words will go the right way again."
This was the poem that Alice read.
JABBERWOCKY.

'Twas brillig, and the slithy toves
Did gyre and gimble in the wabe:
All mimsy were the borogoves,
And the mome raths outgrabe.

"Beware the Jabberwock, my son!
The jaws that bite, the claws that catch!
Beware the Jubjub bird, and shun
The frumious Bandersnatch!"

He took his vorpal sword in hand
Long time the manxome foe he sought --
So rested he by the Tumtum tree,
And stood awhile in thought.

And as in uffish thought he stood,
The Jabberwock, with eyes of flame,
Came whiffling through the tulgey wood,
And burbled as it came!

One, two! One, two! And through and through
The vorpal blade went snicker-snack!
He left it dead, and with its head
He went galumphing back.

"And hast thou slain the Jabberwock?
Come to my arms, my beamish boy!
O frabjous day! Callooh! Callay!"
He chortled in his joy.

'Twas brillig, and the slithy toves
Did gyre and gimble in the wabe;
All mimsy were the borogoves,
And the mome raths outgrabe.

"It seems very pretty," she said when she had finished it, "but it's rather hard to understand!" (You see she didn't like to confess, even to herself, that she couldn't make it out at all.) "Somehow it seems to fill my head with ideas -- only I don't know exactly what they are! However, somebody killed something: that's clear, at any rate -- "

"But oh!" thought Alice, suddenly jumping up, "if I don't make haste I shall have to go back through the Looking-glass, before I've seen what the rest of the house is like! Let's have a look at the garden first!" She was out of the room in a moment and ran downstairs -- or, at least, it wasn't exactly running, but a new invention for getting downstairs quickly and easily, as Alice said to herself. She just kept the tips of her fingers on the handrail, and floated gently down without even touching the stairs with her feet; then she floated on through the hall, and would have gone straight out at the door in the same way, if she hadn't caught hold of the door-post. She was getting a little giddy with so much floating in the air, and was rather glad to find herself walking again in the natural way.

blocks.text: SHE caught the shawl as she spoke, and looked about for the owner: in another moment the White Queen came running wildly through the wood, with both arms stretched out wide, as if she were flying, and Alice very civilly went to meet her with the shawl.
"I'm very glad I happened to be in the way," Alice said, as she helped her to put on her shawl again.

The White Queen only looked at her in a helpless frightened sort of way, and kept repeating something in a whisper to herself that sounded like "Bread-and-butter, bread-and-butter," and Alice felt that if there was to be any conversation at all, she must manage it herself. So she began rather timidly: "Am I addressing the White Queen?"
"Well, yes, if you call that a-dressing," the Queen said. "It isn't my notion of the thing, at all."

Alice thought it would never do to have an argument at the very beginning of their conversation, so she smiled and said, "If your majesty will only tell me the right way to begin, I'll do it as well as I can."
"But I don't want it done at all!" groaned the poor Queen. "I've been a-dressing myself for the last two hours."

It would have been all the better, as it seemed to Alice, if she had got some else to dress her, she was so dreadfully untidy. "Every single thing's crooked," Alice thought to herself, "and she's all over pins! -- May I put your shawl straight for you?" she added aloud.
"I don't know what's the matter with it!" the Queen said, in a melancholy voice. "It's out of temper, I think. I've pinned it here, and I've pinned it there, but there's no pleasing it!"
"It can't go straight, you know, if you pin it all on one side," Alice said, as she gently put it right for her; "and, dear me, what a state your hair is in!"
"The brush has got entangled in it!" the Queen said with a sigh. "And I lost the comb yesterday."

Alice carefully released the brush, and did her best to get the hair into order. "Come, you look rather better now!" she said, after altering most of the pins. "But really you should have a lady's-maid!"
"I'm sure I'll take you with pleasure!" the Queen said. "Twopence a week, and jam every other day."
Alice couldn't help laughing, as she said, "I don't want you to hire me -- and I don't care for jam."
"It's very good jam," said the Queen.
"Well, I don't want any to-day at any rate."
"You couldn't have it if you did want it," the Queen said. "The rule is, jam to-morrow and jam yesterday -- but never jam to-day."
"It must come sometimes to 'jam to-day,' "Alice objected.
"No, it can't," said the Queen. "It's jam every other day: to-day isn't any other day, you know."
"I don't understand you," said Alice. "It's dreadfully confusing!"
"That's the effect of living backward," the Queen said kindly: "it always makes one a little giddy at first -- "
"Living backward!" Alice repeated in great astonishment. "I never heard of such a thing!"
" -- but there's one great advantage in it, that one's memory works both ways."
"I'm sure mine only works one way," Alice remarked.
"I can't remember things before they happen."
"It's a poor sort of memory that only works backward," the Queen remarked.
"What sort of things do you remember best!" Alice ventured to ask.

"Oh, things that happened the week after next," the Queen replied in a careless tone. "For instance, now," she went on, sticking a large piece of plaster on her finger as she spoke, "there's the King's messenger. He's in prison now, being punished: and the trial doesn't even begin till next Wednesday: and of course the crime comes last of all."
"Suppose he never commits the crime?" said Alice.
"That would be all the better, wouldn't it?" the Queen said, as she bound the plaster round her finger with a bit of ribbon.
Alice felt there was no denying that. "Of course it would be all the better," she said: "but it wouldn't be all the better his being punished."
"You're wrong there, at any rate," said the Queen; "were you ever punished?"
"Only for faults," said Alice.
"And you were all the better for it, I know!" the Queen said triumphantly.
"Yes, but then I had done the things I was punished for," said Alice: "that makes all the difference."
"But if you hadn't done them," the Queen said, "that would have been better still; better, and better, and better!" Her voice went higher with each "better," till it got quite to a squeak at last.

blocks.text: "Can you row?" the Sheep asked, handing her a pair of knitting needles as she spoke.

"Yes, a little -- but not on land -- and not with needles -- " Alice was beginning to say, when suddenly the needles turned into oars in her hands, and she found they were in a little boat, gliding along between banks; so there was nothing for it but to do her best.
"Feather!" cried the Sheep, as she took up another pair of needles.

This didn't sound like a remark that needed any answer, so Alice said nothing, but pulled away. There was something very queer about the water, she thought, as every now and then the oars got fast in it, and would hardly come out again.
"Feather! Feather!" the sheep cried again, taking more needles. "You'll be catching a crab directly."
"A dear little crab!" thought Alice. "I should like that."
"Didn't you hear me say 'Feather?'" the Sheep cried angrily, taking up quite a bunch of needles.
"Indeed I did," said Alice: "you've said it very often -- and very loud. Please, where are the crabs?"
"In the water, of course!" said the Sheep, sticking some of the needles into her hair, as her hands were full. "Feather, I say!"
"Why do you say 'Feather' so often?" Alice asked at last, rather vexed. "I'm not a bird!"

"You are," said the Sheep: "you're a little goose." This offended Alice a little, so there was no more conversation for a minute a two, while the boat glided gently on, sometimes among beds of weeds (which made the oars stick fast in the water, worse than ever), and sometimes under trees, but always with the same tall riverbanks frowning over their heads.
"Oh, please! There are some scented rushes!" Alice cried in a sudden transport of delight. "There really are -- and such beauties!"
"You needn't say 'please' to me about 'em," the Sheep said, without looking up from her knitting: "I didn't put 'em there, and I'm not going to take 'em away."
"No, but I meant -- please, may we wait and pick some?" Alice pleaded. "If you don't mind stopping the boat for a minute."
"How am I to stop it?" said the Sheep. "If you leave off rowing, it'll stop of itself."

So the boat was left to drift down the stream as it would, till it glided gently in among the waving rushes. And then the little sleeves were carefully rolled up, and the little arms were plunged in elbow-deep, to get hold of the rushes a good long way down before breaking them off -- and for a while Alice forgot all about the Sheep and the knitting, as she bent over the side of the boat, with just the ends of her tangled hair dipping into the water -- while with bright eager eyes she caught at one bunch after another of the darling scented rushes.

"I only hope the boat won't tipple over!" she said to herself. "Oh, what a lovely one! Only I couldn't quite reach it." And it certainly did seem a little provoking ("almost as if it happened on purpose," she thought) that, though she managed to pick plenty of beautiful rushes as the boat glided by, there was always a more lovely one that she couldn't reach.

"The prettiest are always further!" she said at last, with a sigh at the obstinacy of the rushes in growing so far off, as, with flushed cheeks and dripping hair and hands, she scrambled back into her place, and began to arrange her new-found treasures.

What mattered it to her just then that the rushes had begun to fade, and to lose all their scent and beauty, from the very moment that she picked them? Even real scented rushes, you know, last only a very little while -- and these, being dream-rushes, melted away almost like snow, as they lay in heaps at her feet -- but Alice hardly noticed this, there was so many other curious things to think about.

They hadn't gone much farther before the blade of one of the oars got fast in the water and wouldn't come out again (so Alice explained it afterward), and the consequence was that the handle of it caught her under the chin, and in spite of a series of little shrieks of "Oh, oh, oh!" from poor Alice, it swept her straight off the seat, and down among the heap of rushes.

However, she wasn't a bit hurt, and was soon up again: the Sheep went on with her knitting all the while, just as if nothing had happened. "That was a nice crab you caught!" she remarked, as Alice got back into her place, very much relieved to find herself still in the boat.

"Was it? I didn't see it," said Alice, peeping cautiously over the side of the boat into the dark water. "I wish it hadn't let go -- I should so like a little crab to take home with me!" But the Sheep only laughed scornfully, and went on with her knitting.
"Are there many crabs here?" said Alice.
"Crabs, and all sorts of things," said the Sheep: "plenty of choice, only make up your mind. Now what do you want to buy?"

"To buy!" Alice echoed in a tone that was half astonished and half frightened -- for the oars, and the boat, and the river, had vanished all in a moment, and she was back again in the little dark shop.

blocks.text: I

The dawn laughs out on orient hills
And dances with the diamond rills;
The ambrosial wind but faintly stirs
The silken, beaded gossamers;
In the wide valleys, lone and fair,
Lyrics are piped from limpid air,
And, far above, the pine trees free
Voice ancient lore of sky and sea.
Come, let us fill our hearts straightway
With hope and courage of the day.
II

Noon, hiving sweets of sun and flower,
Has fallen on dreams in wayside bower,
Where bees hold honeyed fellowship
With the ripe blossom of her lip;
All silent are her poppied vales
And all her long Arcadian dales,
Where idleness is gathered up
A magic draught in summer's cup.
Come, let us give ourselves to dreams
By lisping margins of her streams.
III

Adown the golden sunset way
The evening comes in wimple gray;
By burnished shore and silver lake
Cool winds of ministration wake;
O'er occidental meadows far
There shines the light of moon and star,
And sweet, low-tinkling music rings
About the lips of haunted springs.
In quietude of earth and air
'Tis meet we yield our souls to prayer.
